title: Blob Tag
setup: Two players start holding hands as the "blob." Cones mark a 40x40 ft boundary. All others scatter inside.
how: Start with 2 players holding hands as the blob. Everyone else spreads inside the boundary. Coach says "go." Blob moves together. Only the outside hands can tag. Tagged players join the chain. If the chain breaks: that section must freeze for 5 seconds. Last free player wins. Reset immediately and play again. Keep rounds under 3 minutes so energy stays high.
cue: Keep moving. Don't let the blob corner you!
why: Pure movement that builds spatial awareness and agility through play. No instruction needed. Just action.
watch: Chain breaking apart. Enforce the freeze rule. Blob cornering players against a fence. Remind them to use the whole space.
harder: Shrink the boundary each round. Add a second blob once the chain reaches 6 players.
easier: For very young players: no chain. Taggers work solo and tagged players sit out one round.

title: Nuclear Dodgeball
setup: Everyone inside a 30x30 ft square. 2-3 foam balls in play simultaneously.
how: Scatter 3-4 foam balls inside the boundary. On "go," everyone throws at everyone. Hit below the waist = sit in place. Catch a thrown ball while standing = thrower sits. Sitting players can catch a ball to return. Coach calls "reset" after 90 seconds. Everyone stands, play again. Run 4-5 rounds.
cue: Move your feet. Never stand still!
why: Foam balls keep it safe and silly. Lots of throwing, catching, and dodging, it burns off energy, and every kid is moving the whole time.
watch: Head-level throws. Call these out immediately. Players ganging up on one person. Kids who are reluctant: pair them with a ball first.
harder: Reduce the boundary. Add a rule: you can only throw from one knee after catching.
easier: One ball only. Thrower must say the name of who they are throwing at before releasing.

title: Animal Bases
setup: 4 bases in a large square (30 ft apart). Name each base an animal: Lion, Elephant, Monkey, Eagle. One player is "It" in the middle.
how: Name each base an animal before play starts. Make it funny. "It" stands in the middle. Coach calls an animal name. All players sprint to that base. Last player to arrive or anyone tagged mid-sprint becomes the new "It." Change the animal names every 3 rounds to keep attention sharp. Run 6-8 rounds total.
cue: Listen first. Then explode!
why: Kids have to listen, then go. Lots of short sprints and quick starts, and the silly names keep the little ones laughing.
watch: Players clustering at one base. Add a 3-player max per base rule. "It" not being active. Give them a 5-second window to chase.
harder: Add a penalty base. Players at the penalty base must do 5 hops before rejoining. Coach calls TWO animals simultaneously.
easier: Walk only. No tagging. Last player to the base becomes "It."

title: Freeze Tag Baseball
setup: 2-3 players are "it." Tagged players freeze in a batting stance. Untagged players can unfreeze teammates by crawling through their legs.
how: Choose 2-3 taggers. Tagged players freeze in a batting stance. Feet shoulder-width, slight bend, hands up. Untagged players can unfreeze teammates by crawling through their legs. Rotate taggers every 90 seconds. Run 3-4 rounds. After the game: ask players "what does a good batting stance feel like?" Let them answer.
cue: Stay low when you run. Like you're ducking under something!
why: Freezing in a batting stance sneaks in athletic positioning without making it feel like a drill.
watch: Frozen players not holding the stance. Gentle reminder. Crawling players getting kicked. Enforce that frozen players stay still.
harder: Frozen players must hold a fielding ready position instead of batting stance. Add a second unfreeze method: partner throws a ball to them and they catch it.
easier: No crawling unfreeze. A teammate just taps you to unfreeze.

title: Bandits
setup: Each player tucks a pinnie or flag into the back of their waistband. Boundary 40x40 ft.
how: Each player tucks a pinnie into their waistband with about 12 inches hanging out. On "go," everyone protects their own flag while stealing others. Stolen flag goes in your hand. You keep playing. If your flag is stolen: you are out and cheer from the sideline. Last player with a flag wins. Play 3-4 rounds of 60-90 seconds.
cue: Change direction fast. Protect your flag!
why: Develops change-of-direction agility and spatial awareness. Competitive without being physically aggressive.
watch: Grabbing jerseys or shorts instead of flags. Players just running away instead of competing. Reduce boundary.
harder: Reduce boundary. Add: if you have 3 flags you must give one back.
easier: Team bandits. Two teams, collect your team color flags only.

title: Shark Island
setup: Scatter 4-5 bases around the field as islands. 2-3 players are "sharks." All others are swimmers.
how: Mark 4-5 bases as islands. Choose 2 sharks. Swimmers move between islands. Max 2 per island. Third player arriving must leave immediately. Tagged players become sharks. Sharks cannot stand on islands. Run for 90 seconds, then count remaining swimmers. New round with new sharks. 4 rounds.
cue: Keep your head up. Know where every island is!
why: Kids keep their heads up and make quick choices about where to run. Lots of movement, lots of decisions, no standing in line.
watch: Three players piling on one island. Enforce the 2-player max firmly. Sharks guarding one island without moving.
harder: Reduce to 3 islands. Add a time limit on islands. Max 10 seconds per stay.
easier: No tagging. Sharks count to 5 when pointing at a swimmer in the water; that swimmer becomes a shark.

title: Scatter Grounders
setup: Coach at center. Players scattered in a loose semicircle 20-30 ft away. Use tennis balls for younger groups.
how: Coach stands in the center with a bucket of 10-15 tennis balls. Players spread out in a loose semicircle. No lines. Coach rolls one grounder at a time in unpredictable directions. Players call "mine" and field it, then roll or toss back to coach. As soon as one ball is fielded, coach rolls the next to a different player. No waiting. Keep moving. Keep it flowing for the whole block.
cue: Get in front of it. Field it with your body, not just your glove.
why: Nobody knows where the next ball is going, so every kid stays ready. No lines means far more touches than waiting for a turn.
watch: Players standing straight up waiting. Two players going for the same ball. Reinforce the "mine" call. Players throwing back too hard. Keep it safe.
harder: Mix in pop-ups randomly. Move players closer together so communication is required. Add a decision: after fielding, player must call where they would throw.
easier: Slow rollers only. Shorter distance to the coach.

title: Two-Team Ball Pick-Up
setup: Two teams on opposite ends of the field. Scatter 20-30 tennis balls randomly in the middle zone.
how: Scatter 20-30 tennis balls in a central zone. Two teams start at opposite ends 30 feet away. On "go," each player runs to the zone, picks up ONE ball, carries it back to their bucket, and returns for another. No throwing. Carry only. No taking balls from the opponent's bucket. After 60 seconds, count balls. Team with most wins. Play 4 rounds.
cue: Bend your knees. Get low to the ground!
why: Getting low to pick up the ball is built into the game, and the race makes kids hustle without being told to.
watch: Players grabbing more than one ball. Blocking opponents. Keep it competitive but clean.
harder: Add a rule: you must field the ball with a two-hand scooping motion (not picking up). Require players to touch a cone at the far end before returning.
easier: No time limit. Just count who collects more in a relaxed format.

title: Four Corners Fielding
setup: Players at four bases. Ball starts at home. Infield-sized square.
how: One player at each base. Ball starts at home. Home throws to third, third throws to second, second throws to first, first throws home. Count how many error-free trips around the horn in 2 minutes. Then reverse direction. Add a rule: before throwing, fielder must call the base they are throwing to. Rest 30 seconds. Compete against the previous score.
cue: Catch it, find your target, throw. Not the other way around.
why: Lots of catches and throws with no lines. Calling the base makes kids look before they let it go.
watch: Players throwing before they have a grip. Fielders not calling the base. Enforce it.
harder: Add a fifth player as a runner going around the bases. Fielders must beat the runner. Add a required one-hop catch at each base.
easier: Shorter distances. Use tennis balls. Allow a 2-second hold before throwing.

title: Goalie Grounders
setup: Two cones 6 feet apart as a goal. Fielder stands in front of goal. Coach/partner 15 feet away.
how: Set two cones 6 feet apart as a goal. Fielder stands in front of the goal in ready position. Partner kneels 15 feet away with a bucket of balls. Partner rolls one grounder at a time. Aiming for the gap. Fielder blocks it. 10 attempts, record how many get through. Switch roles. Compete. Progress: partner can roll to either side at random.
cue: Slide your feet, don't reach. Move your body to the ball.
why: The goal gives instant feedback: the ball gets through or it does not. Kids tend to move their feet more when there is something to defend.
watch: Fielder reaching with one hand. Must get body in front. Fielder watching the partner's hand instead of the ball. Standing too upright.
harder: Widen the goal to 8 feet. Faster rolls. Add backhanders by rolling wide to the glove-hand side.
easier: Narrow the goal to 4 feet. Slower rolls. Fielder can use hands only (no glove).

title: Overthrow Chaos
setup: Full infield. Coach hits or rolls balls. Runners on bases.
how: Full infield with runners. Coach hits or rolls a ball. Fielder makes the play. But coach has secretly pre-decided: 30% of plays result in an overthrow (coach tosses a second ball past the base immediately). Fielders must read the overthrow and back up, cut it, or let it go. Runners advance on overthrows. Debrief each play: "What was the smart read?"
cue: What's the smart play, not just the first play?
why: Overthrows happen a lot in youth games. Practicing the messy version gives kids reps at backing up, cutting, and reading the ball.
watch: No one backing up first base. Assign a specific player. Cutoff man not getting in position before the throw.
harder: Add a second simultaneous overthrow. Live runners on all bases.
easier: Pre-announce whether an overthrow is coming. Builds the habit before adding the surprise element.

title: Pop Fly Zone
setup: 3-4 outfielders spread in a zone. Coach hits pop-ups randomly. No assigned player per ball.
how: 3-4 outfielders spread in a zone. Coach hits 15 pop-ups randomly. No pattern. Players communicate: caller says "mine" loudly twice. Everyone else says "yours" and clears. If no one calls it: let it fall, then talk about who should have had it. Mix in line drives and shallow bloopers. After every 5 balls, ask: who should have had that one?
cue: Call it early. Loud and twice.
why: Fly ball communication is hard for young players. This gives lots of chances to call the ball out loud with teammates around.
watch: Late calls (after already camped under it). Players not clearing when someone calls it. One player dominating all calls.
harder: Add an infielder going back on the ball. The outfielder coming in has priority and calls the infielder off. Add sun field: players shield their eyes with the glove.
easier: Coach points at the intended fielder before hitting. Reduce to 2 outfielders.

title: Soft Hands Wall Drill
setup: Player stands 6-8 feet from a flat wall. No glove.
how: Player stands 6-8 feet from a flat wall. NO glove. Throw a tennis ball against the wall. Aim at a target marked with tape. Field the rebound bare-handed with two hands. Feel the ball land softly. Hands give backward on contact. 20 reps bare-handed. Then put the glove on and take 10 more reps. Compare the feel.
cue: Give with the ball. Let your hands absorb it.
why: Without a glove, kids feel right away if they are stabbing at the ball or giving with it. The wall gives lots of reps fast.
watch: Snatching at the ball instead of receiving it. One-handed catches. Standing too far back. Get closer.
harder: Step back to 12-15 feet. Throw harder so the rebound is faster. Add lateral movement: throw angled so rebound requires a shuffle step.
easier: Bounce the ball off the floor instead of the wall. Slower and more predictable.

title: Two-Location Tee Work
gear: Tee, balls, net or open field
setup: Tee set up with two marked positions: inside (tee moved forward and in) and outside (tee moved back and out). Alternate randomly.
how: Set up tee at the inside location (forward, close to hitter). Hit 5 balls. Move tee to outside location (back, away from hitter). Hit 5 balls. Now: call location before each swing and alternate randomly. 20 swings total. Inside: hitter should contact the ball out front and drive it pull-side. Outside: hitter should contact deeper and drive it to the opposite field.
cue: Inside: hit it out front. Outside: let it travel and drive it the other way.
why: Moving the tee makes the hitter adjust their contact point instead of grooving one spot. Start with one location for beginners, then mix it up as they get comfortable.
watch: Hitter not adjusting their contact point. Swinging at the same spot regardless of tee location. Lunging on outside pitches. Pulling the outside pitch.
harder: Randomize without calling location. Just move the tee and let them adjust. Add a third location: middle of the plate.
easier: One location only per session for beginners. Call the location 5 seconds before swinging.

title: Wiffle Ball No-Glove Game
gear: Wiffle balls, plastic bats, bases at 25-30 ft
setup: 3 teams. Triangle field: home + 2 bases at 25-30 ft. Coach pitches lob tosses. No gloves.
how: Three equal teams. Triangle field: home plate plus two bases at 25-30 feet. Coach pitches lob tosses. One per batter. Batter hits, runs to any base. No fielding gloves. Fielders must catch bare-handed or field with two hands. After 3 outs (one out per batter), rotate teams. Ask "Where's the play?" before every pitch. Run 3 full rotations.
cue: Where's the play before the ball is hit?
why: Wiffle balls and no gloves take the fear out of it. The small field means kids can actually make plays, and everyone bats a lot.
watch: Fielders trying to throw runners out at bases they can't reach. Redirect to the base they can make. Batters not running on contact.
harder: Add a designated short fielder. Batters must call which base they are running to before hitting.
easier: No outs. Everyone bats and runs every time. Just play for fun.

title: Random Front Toss
setup: Tosser sits or kneels behind an L-screen 12-20 feet in front of the hitter. Balls marked H (high) or L (low) in a bucket.
how: Tosser sits or kneels behind an L-screen 12-20 feet in front of the hitter (closer for younger players so the toss stays accurate). Before each toss, the tosser pulls a ball from a bucket marked H or L with a sharpie. Hitter cannot see the selection. Tosser tosses firmly, underhand. Hitter reads and adjusts. 20 tosses. After 10: add a fake toss now and then. Hitter must not swing.
cue: See it early. Decide early.
why: Hitters have to read the height and adjust instead of knowing what is coming. Kids like the guessing game, and the fakes teach them to wait.
watch: Hitter committing to the swing before the ball reaches the zone. No adjustment between high and low. Swinging the same path regardless.
harder: Add inside/outside as additional variables. Use a pitch recognition device or colored balls.
easier: Announce high or low before each toss. Fixed location only.

title: Mini Home Run Derby
gear: Tee or coach pitch, soft balls or wiffle balls
setup: Mark a home run line with cones in the outfield. Coach pitches or players hit off tee. Each player gets 5 swings.
how: Mark a home run line with cones. 60 feet for younger players, 80-90 feet for older. Coach pitches or hitters hit off tee. Each player gets 5 swings per turn. Ball over the cone line = home run (1 point). Ball in play but not over = single (0.5 points). Team with most points after two full rotations wins. Announce the score after each turn.
cue: Drive through the ball. Finish your swing.
why: Kids love it. Swinging to hit it far is fun, and a target line gives every swing a clear goal.
watch: Uppercut swings creating pop-ups. Cue "drive through the ball." Players not swinging hard. Competition context should naturally fix this.
harder: Move the cone line back. Add a bonus: 2 points for hitting a designated target zone.
easier: No competition. Just hit and count home runs individually. Closer cone line.

title: Pepper
setup: 3 fielders stand 10-12 feet from batter in a line. Batter tries to hit controlled grounders back to fielders.
how: Three fielders stand in a line 10-12 feet from the batter. Batter uses a short, controlled swing to hit grounders directly at fielders. Fielder who catches it immediately tosses back underhand. Batter redirects the next toss at a different fielder. No big swings. This is bat control. Rotate batter after 10 consecutive contacts. If the batter hits it too hard and a fielder can't catch it: batter gives up their turn.
cue: Short swing, stay through the ball.
why: A classic for a reason: fast reps, bat control for the hitter, and quick hands for the fielders, all in a small space.
watch: Full swings. Enforce the short-swing rule. Fielders tossing too hard back to the batter. Batter aiming only at one fielder.
harder: Add a rule: batter must alternate which fielder they hit to. Shrink the distance to 8 feet.
easier: Fielder just rolls the ball to the batter instead of tossing. No catch required on the return.

title: Count-Based Hitting
setup: Real or simulated count starts at 0-0. Coach announces count before each pitch.
how: Coach announces the count before each pitch: "You're 0-2." Pitcher throws accordingly. Trying to expand the zone on 0-2, throw a strike on 3-0. Hitter adjusts approach by count. After each at-bat (3 pitches), debrief: "What was your job in that count?" Let the hitter answer. Coach adds only what was missed. Run 3 at-bats per hitter. Count live pitches toward each pitcher's daily limit.
cue: What's your job in this count?
why: Gives hitters a plan for each count. Talking it through after each at-bat helps kids start thinking about the count on their own.
watch: Hitters swinging the same way regardless of count. Pitchers not adjusting to count either.
harder: Call a situation + count: "Bases loaded, 2-2." Live runners. Real consequences.
easier: Two counts only: hitter's count (2-0) vs pitcher's count (0-2). Ask which one before pitching.

title: Wall Target Throwing
gear: Tennis balls, tape targets on wall
setup: Mark 3 targets on a wall with tape: low (knee height), middle (chest), high (shoulder). Start 20 feet away.
how: Mark three tape targets on a wall: knee height, chest height, shoulder height. Label them 1 (low), 2 (middle), 3 (high). Player stands 20 feet away. Player calls the target out loud before throwing. 5 throws at each target, 15 total. Score: direct hit = 3 pts, within 6 inches = 1 pt. Move to 30 feet and repeat. Keep a running score across sessions.
cue: Pick a target. Throw to a spot, not at a person.
why: Calling a target before the throw gives kids something outside their body to aim at. The score gives instant feedback, and they can chase their own record.
watch: Player throwing without calling the target first. Enforce the habit. Player looking at their arm instead of the target.
harder: Shrink the targets. Add a time limit. Must throw within 5 seconds of calling target.
easier: Just two targets: high and low. Shorter distance. Larger targets.

title: Partner Random Distance
setup: Partners start 20 feet apart. Coach calls random distances.
how: Partners start 20 feet apart. Coach calls a distance: "30 feet." Both pairs adjust simultaneously. Coach gives 10 seconds to get to position, then calls "throw." After 3 throws at that distance, coach calls a completely different distance: "15 feet." Mix far and close distances randomly. 20 throws total. The randomness is the point. Players must calibrate effort every single throw.
cue: Hit your partner in the chest from every distance.
why: Kids have to figure out how hard to throw every single time, which is closer to game throws than same-distance catch.
watch: Players throwing max effort at every distance. Short throws sailing over the partner. Chest-high is the goal.
harder: Coach calls the distance right as partners are mid-throw. They must adjust the next one. Add a target at each distance.
easier: Three set distances only: short (20), medium (40), long (60). Announce which one before they move.

title: Crow Hop Relay
setup: 3 relay stations 40 feet apart. Two teams race.
how: Three stations 40 feet apart. Two equal teams run parallel. Ball starts at station 1. Player at station 1 crow hops (a quick hop onto the throwing-side foot, then a step toward the target with the glove-side foot) and throws to station 2. Station 2 catches, crow hops, throws to station 3. Station 3 throws back to station 1. Every throw must include the crow hop. No crow hop = that team loses the point for that relay. Team with most completed relays in 3 minutes wins.
cue: Crow hop before every outfield throw. Always.
why: Relay races add urgency and teamwork to outfield throws. The crow hop gives kids a simple footwork pattern for longer throws.
watch: Players throwing without crow hop. Enforce it strictly, that's the whole point. Crow hop going in the wrong direction.
harder: Add a fourth station. Start each relay with a ground ball the first player must field.
easier: Practice the crow hop footwork without a ball first. Walk through: hop onto the throwing-side foot, step toward the target with the glove-side foot, then throw.

title: Target Bucket
gear: Tennis balls, bucket or trash can
setup: Bucket or trash can at various positions. Start 15 feet away.
how: Place a bucket or large trash can at 15 feet. Player throws 5 tennis balls trying to land them in the bucket. Count direct makes. Move to 20 feet. Throw 5 more. Move to 30 feet. 5 more. Then 40 feet. After reaching max distance: come back to 20 feet for a final 10 throws. Precision round. Keep a session record: best score at each distance.
cue: High arc to get it in from far away. Flat throws miss short.
why: The bucket is an easy target to aim at, and kids figure out the arc on their own. Scoring makes it a game.
watch: Flat throws on longer distances: cue "arc it up." Players rushing throws.
harder: Make the bucket smaller (a coffee can at close range). Add a 10-second time limit per throw.
easier: Underhand toss only. Bucket at 8 feet. Use a large laundry basket as the target.

title: Chest Target Catch Streak
setup: Partners 20 feet apart, standing. Receiver holds the glove at the chest as a target before every throw.
how: Partners stand 20 feet apart. Receiver shows a glove target at the chest before each throw. Easy, comfortable throws. A clean catch at the chest counts. Count the streak out loud as a pair. A drop, a bad throw, or a chase resets the count to zero. After a streak of 10, both step back 5 feet. Keep it under about 40 feet for younger players. Stop anytime an arm is sore.
cue: Hit the glove. Catch it with two hands.
why: Turns regular catch into a game with a goal. Kids aim at a small target and count streaks, which keeps attention on catching and accuracy instead of on how the arm moves.
watch: Throwing hard to show off. The goal is catchable throws. One-handed stabs. Anyone rubbing their arm or saying it hurts: stop and tell a parent.
harder: Receiver moves the glove target after each catch (left, right, high, low). Add a quick-release rule: throw within 3 seconds of the catch.
easier: Shorter distance (10-15 feet). Foam or tennis ball. Count to 5 instead of 10.

title: Around the Horn Competition
setup: Players at each infield position. Time starts when first throw is made.
how: Players at each infield base. Ball starts at home. On "go": throw 3B → 2B → 1B → C → 3B. Count time with a stopwatch. Record the best error-free time. Then reverse: C → 1B → 2B → 3B → C. Add rule: each fielder must call the base before throwing. Challenge: can the team beat their record? Celebrate when they do.
cue: Catch it, find your target, release. Don't hold it.
why: A real pregame routine that kids enjoy racing. The stopwatch adds pressure in a fun way, and chasing the team record keeps everyone locked in.
watch: Throws before the fielder has a secure grip. No verbal call before throwing. Fielder ball-watching instead of getting in position for the next throw.
harder: Add a baserunner trying to beat the throw. Require one-hop throws at each station.
easier: Remove the stopwatch. Just make error-free throws around the horn before adding speed.

title: First Step Competition
setup: Players in batting stance at home plate. Coach faces the pitcher's mound with a ball.
how: Players in batting stance at home plate. Coach stands at pitcher's mound holding a ball. Coach does NOT say go. Instead, coach moves the ball (lifts glove, drops arm, or steps toward the plate). Players react to the ball movement with their first step toward first base. Race to see who gets there first. Debrief: "What did you see that made you go?" Run 10 reads.
cue: React to the ball moving. Not to a sound.
why: A reaction game. Kids watch for a movement and go, and quick first steps help everywhere on the bases.
watch: Players going on the coach's voice instead of movement. False starts from anticipating. First step going backward. It must be toward first.
harder: Coach sometimes flinches without moving the ball. Anyone who goes on the fake sits out one rep. Then run it from first base, with runners leaving when your league's rules allow.
easier: Let players watch the coach's hand only. No full body read yet.

title: Read the Ball Baserunning
setup: Runners on base. Coach or player hits to various positions.
how: Runners on base. Coach hits or rolls to various positions. Runners go on contact with no instructions. After each rep: runner must explain the read out loud. "The ball went to the outfield and I saw it land. I went to third." Coach asks one follow-up question. Never corrects unless safety is an issue. 10 reads per runner.
cue: Tag up or go early. Which read do you need?
why: Saying the read out loud makes kids notice what they saw. Over time the read tends to get quicker and more automatic.
watch: Runners waiting for a coach to wave them. No waving in this drill. Runners not watching the ball all the way.
harder: Add real fielders trying to make plays. Add a two-out situation where runners go on contact.
easier: Coach describes the situation before hitting: "I'm going to hit this to left field. What do you think you should do?"

title: Secondary Lead Reads
setup: Runner at first base. Pitcher/coach in the mound area. Catcher at the plate. Use only where leads are legal: Little League 12U and younger does not allow leads, and in fastpitch softball runners leave on the release.
how: Runner at first. Coach in the pitcher's mound area. Catcher at plate. Every pitch: runner begins 2 secondary shuffle steps as the ball leaves the pitcher's hand. Not when it crosses the plate. By the time the ball reaches the catcher, the runner should already be mid-shuffle. Ball in the dirt: runner goes. Ball caught cleanly: return to first. Pitch in the air: freeze and read. No instruction during reps. Just watch. After 15 reads, ask the runner to describe the rule they were using.
cue: Shuffle as the ball leaves the pitcher's hand, not when it crosses the plate.
why: A good secondary lead helps runners react to balls in the dirt. Where leads are legal, this gives lots of reads in a short time.
watch: Runner taking the secondary lead too early. Must wait for the pitch. Runner not shuffling. Just standing still.
harder: Add a real steal attempt. Runner can try to steal on any pitch they read as stolen base opportunity.
easier: Coach announces "dirt" or "clean" before each pitch. Runner just practices the footwork response.

title: Rounding Bases Race
setup: Two players race from home, around all four bases, back to home.
how: Two players race simultaneously from home plate. Both must round all four bases and return to home. Player who finishes first gets one point. But only if they hit the inside corner of each bag (touched the front-inside corner). Check this: coach stands at second base and watches. Play a set of 5 races. Player with most valid wins takes the series.
cue: Hit the inside corner of each bag. Never run in a straight line.
why: A good turn keeps runners moving fast through the base instead of slowing down to change direction. Racing makes kids want to do it right.
watch: Players running straight lines. Reinforce the arc path. Missing the inside corner to save time. Penalize this.
harder: Add a cone a few feet outside the baseline, about 15 feet before each base, to mark the start of the turn. Runners must stay outside the cone.
easier: Walk the correct arc path first. Use cones to mark the correct line before racing.

title: Three-Base Circuit
setup: Runner at first base. Coach hits the ball. Live fielders in the field.
how: Runner at first. Coach hits or rolls to various field positions. Live fielders in play. Runner reads contact and makes decisions without being told. After each rep: runner describes their read: "I saw it go through the infield so I went to third." Coach asks one question only: "What did you see that made you hold?" or "What would you do differently?" Run 8-10 circuits.
cue: What did you see that made you go?
why: The question after the play is where the learning shows up. Kids start to notice what they see before they run.
watch: Runner making decisions before the ball is hit. Not looking at the ball while running.
harder: Add a second runner at third. Creates a different set of reads. Time the runner and fielders.
easier: Coach hits specific balls and tells the runner the expected outcome before the play.

title: Three-Team Small-Sided Game
gear: Bases at 45-50 ft, wiffle or soft balls
setup: 3 equal teams. Compressed diamond at 45-50 ft base paths. Coach pitches. Two teams playing, one resting. Rotate every 6-8 minutes.
how: Three equal teams. Compressed diamond: bases at 45-50 feet. Coach pitches. Two teams play, one rests. Resting team watches and asks "where's the play?" before each pitch. After 8 minutes or 3 outs (whichever comes first): rotate. The resting team calls the next team in. Keep score across rotations. Before every single pitch: coach asks any fielder "Where's the play?"
cue: Where's the play before the ball is hit?
why: Three teams means short waits and lots of at-bats. The small field makes throws doable at this age.
watch: Fielders not pre-setting before the pitch. Batters not running on contact. Resting team disengaging.
harder: Move bases to 55 feet. Add a situational rule: if a runner is on second with no outs, batter must drive them in or the team loses a point.
easier: No outs. Just play and rotate every 5 minutes. Reduce to one-pitch at-bats.

title: Hit and Run: No Fielders
gear: Tee or coach pitch, soft balls, bases
setup: No fielders. All players are hitters and runners. Short base paths (40 ft). Two teams alternate.
how: No fielders. Two teams alternate. One bats, one waits at a separate area. Batter hits (tee or coach pitch), runs to first, continues running bases as far as possible in 10 seconds before coach calls "stop." Points = number of bases reached. After the timed 10 seconds, coach calls score and batter returns. Next batter up immediately. High pace. No waiting.
cue: Run hard every time. Don't stop until someone tells you to!
why: Young players need lots of swings and lots of running. Skipping fielding at this age keeps the energy up and the waiting down.
watch: Batters stopping at first out of habit. Batters running without urgency. Create energy.
harder: Add a ghost fielder rule: if the ball goes less than 20 feet, it's an automatic out.
easier: Let the child just run the bases freely first, forward and around all four, before adding a hit.

title: Situational Game
setup: Full field. Coach places runners in specific situations before each at-bat: runner on second with one out, bases loaded two outs, etc.
how: Coach pre-sets a situation before each at-bat: "Runner on second. One out." Live pitching. Both teams play it out for real. No restarts unless safety. After 3 outs, coach resets a new situation for the next half-inning. After every 2 situations, ask the defense: "What was the most important thing to prevent in that situation?"
cue: What does defense want to prevent here? What does offense want to do?
why: Kids play out real situations instead of hearing about them. The quick debrief after each one connects the situation to the right play.
watch: Defense not communicating pre-pitch. Offense not adjusting approach to the situation.
harder: Add a consequence: if defense executes the correct play, they get an extra out. If offense executes correctly (bunt, sac fly, etc.) they get an extra run.
easier: Coach announces both teams' strategies before the inning starts.

title: Wiffle Ball Tournament
setup: Round-robin format. 3-4 teams of 2-3 players. Short base paths (30-40 ft). Pitch to your own team for fairness.
how: 3-4 teams of 2-3 players. Pitch to your own team for fairness. Throws your own team strikes. Play 5-inning games with a 5-minute time limit. Keep real score on a board visible to all players. Standings posted after each round. Tournament bracket for final two teams. Coach stays out of the game. This is theirs.
cue: Play like it counts. Because it does.
why: Kids care about standings. A tournament makes every at-bat matter to them, and the coach stepping back lets them own the game.
watch: Teams disputing calls. Appoint one player from the resting team as umpire. Players losing interest because the score is lopsided. Mercy rule: max 5 runs per inning.
harder: Real pitching instead of self-pitching. Add baserunning rules: can only advance on contact.
easier: No score. Just play. Rotate teams freely without a formal structure.

title: Pitcher-Fielder Game
setup: One player is the pitcher. One is a fielder. One is a runner at home.
how: Three rotating roles: pitcher (throws to a base), fielder (at a base ready to receive and tag), runner (at home). Coach hits or rolls a ball into play. Pitcher fields and throws to the fielder. Runner sprints. Fielder catches and tags. Score: out = pitcher+fielder get a point, safe = runner gets a point. Rotate after each play. Play to 10 points.
cue: Beat the runner. Throw to the base, not to the player.
why: Accuracy under a little time pressure, with an instant result: out or safe. More game-like than throwing from a standstill.
watch: Fielder throwing to the player instead of the base. Runner giving up on a play.
harder: Add a live hit. Batter gets to hit instead of coach rolling. Multiple runners.
easier: No runner. Just practice the pitcher-to-fielder throw sequence 10 times before adding competition.

title: Water Balloon Throw Contest
setup: Two teams on opposite sides of a center line. Pre-fill balloons before practice.
how: Pre-fill 20-30 balloons before practice. Two teams on opposite sides of a center line. On "go": three minutes of throwing balloons to the opposite side. When a balloon hits the ground on a side: it stays there. When time is called: count balloons on each side. Team with fewer on their side wins. Run 2-3 rounds. Coach stands back and lets them play.
cue: Throw it with your whole body. Not just your arm!
why: Pure fun. Kids throw with full effort and big body movement when they are excited, and it makes a great closer on a hot day.
watch: Players throwing at faces. Set a "below the shoulders" rule before starting. Hoarding balloons instead of throwing.
harder: Players must throw with their non-dominant arm. Add a rule: you must crow hop before each throw.
easier: Just throw. No competition. Let them explore for 2 minutes before adding the game.

title: Baserunning Chaos Game
setup: All players start at home. Coach or player at pitcher's mound with a ball.
how: All players start at home plate. Coach or player at the mound rolls or hits any ball anywhere in the field. All players run simultaneously and try to advance as many bases as possible. Fielders try to get the ball and hold runners. No outs. Just maximum bases. After each play, count total bases advanced by all runners combined. Compete to beat the total each round.
cue: Run until you see the ball under control. Then decide.
why: Teaches kids to run hard and then read when to stop. Many young runners play it safe; this gives them permission to be aggressive in practice.
watch: Runners stopping at a base without reading whether they can advance. Fielders throwing to runners instead of bases.
harder: Add real fielders who can make force plays at bases. Two separate groups of runners. Which group gets more total bases?
easier: Slow roll only. Gives runners more time to read and react.

title: 21 Outs Game
setup: Two teams. The game ends when 21 total outs have been made (three and a half innings).
how: Two teams. Real baseball rules. Coach pitches or player pitches. Walks count as singles (no slow-down from walks). Keep real score. Play until 21 total outs have been made (three and a half innings). Count player pitches toward daily limits. Between innings: coach makes exactly ONE team-level observation. Not directed at any individual player. Keep it to 30 seconds. Emphasis: play the game, figure it out.
cue: Play the game. Figure it out.
why: Real game reps in practice. Kids get to play the game and figure things out without stopping for instruction.
watch: Coach over-coaching between innings. Hold to one observation. Players not tracking the count of outs.
harder: Player pitching instead of coach. Add a game-level consequence: winner gets to choose the next drill.
easier: Two innings only. One out per batter to speed it up.

title: Flat Ground Spot Work
setup: Pitcher on flat ground, catcher or net at your league's pitching distance. Catcher sets up target in four zones: up-in, up-out, down-in, down-out.
how: Catcher sets up at your league's pitching distance (46 feet in Little League Majors, shorter in younger divisions). Catcher shows four targets: up-in, up-out, down-in, down-out. Hold the glove for 3 full seconds in the target before the pitcher winds up. Pitcher calls the target before throwing. 20 pitches total. 5 per zone. Track: hit the target (within 6 inches of glove) vs. miss. Find the worst zone and throw 5 extra to that zone. Count every pitch toward the day's pitch count.
cue: Pick a corner, see the corner, throw to the corner.
why: Aiming at a spot gives the pitcher a simple goal and instant feedback. We keep feedback on the result, not the delivery. Delivery work belongs with a qualified pitching coach.
watch: Not calling the target before throwing. Pitchers trying to throw harder instead of hitting the spot. Any arm pain: stop for the day.
harder: Add a batter standing in the box. Doesn't swing, just gives visual context. Reduce the target size.
easier: Catcher holds a large glove target flat. Easier visual. Shorter distance (35 feet).

title: Stork Balance Challenge
setup: Players spread out on flat ground. No ball needed.
how: Players spread out. On "go," everyone lifts one knee toward hip height and holds. Anyone who touches down sits and cheers. Last player standing wins the round. Switch legs each round. Add challenges: eyes closed, catch a soft toss while balancing, or turn the head side to side. 5 rounds.
cue: Pick a spot and stare at it. Stay tall.
why: A fun balance game for pitchers and everyone else. We treat balance as a general athletic skill here, not a delivery lesson. Delivery coaching belongs with a qualified pitching coach.
watch: Players holding their breath or locking the standing knee. Kids who wobble a lot: let them touch a fence first and build up.
harder: Eyes closed. Catch a soft toss while balancing. Balance on a folded towel.
easier: Hold for 5 seconds. Fingertips on a fence or a partner's shoulder.

title: Target Strike Competition
gear: Strike zone target or catcher, ball
setup: Two pitchers alternate. Each gets 10 pitches. Call balls and strikes against a strike zone target.
how: Two pitchers alternate. Each gets 10 pitches into a strike zone target or catcher. Score: strike = 1 pt, ball = 0. Most strikes in 10 pitches wins the round. Play 3 rounds. Between rounds: each pitcher identifies their worst zone from that round. Final round: each pitcher declares which zone they are attacking before each pitch.
cue: Throw it like you don't care. Throw through the target.
why: A simple strike contest makes command practice fun and gives each pitcher a score to beat. Keep it about hitting the target, not about changing the delivery.
watch: Pitchers trying to throw too hard to impress. Accuracy only. Pitchers not honoring the zone declaration.
harder: Reduce the strike zone target size. Add a catcher who frames aggressively to create closer calls.
easier: Pitch to a large bucket or trash can as the target. Distance reduced to 40 feet.

title: Closing Circle Question
setup: End of practice huddle. Players in a circle around the coach.
how: Players in a circle. Coach asks exactly ONE question. Not a statement, a question. Examples: "What was the hardest decision you made today?" or "What would you do differently on one play?" Players go around the circle. No evaluation from the coach. Coach says only "thanks" or "good." If a player says "I don't know," wait 5 seconds in silence before moving on. Silence is okay.
cue: One question. Honest answers. Done.
why: Ending with one question gets kids to think back on what they did. The coach staying quiet during answers keeps it safe to be honest.
watch: Coach turning a question into a mini-lecture. Players giving answers they think the coach wants to hear.
harder: Players ask each other questions instead of coach asking. A player leads the closing circle.
easier: Coach provides two options: "Did this practice feel more like work or more like a game?" Yes/no questions for younger players.

title: Mistake Ritual
setup: After any error in practice. This is a team habit, not a punishment.
how: Teach the ritual at the start of the season as a deliberate team activity. Step 1: agree on the physical move (shake out the hands, adjust the hat; the team chooses together). Step 2: agree on the words ("next play," said by the team). Step 3: agree on the forward focus gesture (point to the next base, or look to the outfield). Practice it: have a player intentionally drop a ball, then perform the ritual 10 times. Keep using it until it feels automatic.
cue: Shake it off. Next play.
why: A shared ritual makes mistakes normal and gives kids a quick way to move on. It is simple, it is theirs, and it keeps the team together after an error.
watch: Coach rushing the ritual by moving on before the player finishes it. Players laughing at a teammate during the ritual. Redirect this immediately.
harder: Add a team response after the individual ritual. Whole team says "next play" together.
easier: Just the words, "next play," with no physical ritual yet. Add the physical component after the words feel natural.

title: Pre-Practice Visualization
setup: Players seated or standing quietly, eyes closed. Coach speaks slowly.
how: Players sit or stand quietly. Eyes closed. Coach speaks slowly and specifically: "You are standing at the plate. See the pitcher. See the ball in their glove. See their wind-up. The ball leaves the hand. You pick it up immediately. You see it spin. You see it come into your zone. You swing. You feel the contact. You watch the ball go where you aimed." Two to three minutes. One player shares what they saw.
cue: See it first. Then do it.
why: Imagery is a common sport psychology tool with some research support, mostly with older athletes. For kids, keep it short, specific, and optional.
watch: Players laughing or fidgeting. This is normal at first. Give it three sessions before judging engagement.
harder: Players lead their own visualization silently without coach guidance. Add a game-situation context.
easier: Just 2 minutes. Just the at-bat. No full imagery sequence.

title: Effort Score Check-In
setup: Coach calls the team in after a drill.
how: After any drill, coach calls everyone in. "Hold up fingers for your effort score. 1 to 5. Be honest." On the count of three, everyone shows their number. Coach does not evaluate the numbers. Coach asks one player who showed a 3: "What would a 5 look like on that drill?" Let them answer fully. Coach says "got it" and moves on.
cue: What would a 5 look like?
why: Kids rate themselves instead of waiting for the coach to judge. "What would a 5 look like?" points them forward instead of backward.
watch: Players showing 5 without honest reflection. Coach reacting to low numbers negatively. It must be safe to be honest.
harder: Players ask each other the question instead of coach.
easier: Just two options. Thumbs up or thumbs down. Build to the number system.

title: Free Swing Tee Station
gear: Tee, foam ball or wiffle ball
setup: Individual tee stations. Soft ball on tee. Kids hit into a net or open space. No instruction initially.
how: Individual tee stations. Foam ball or wiffle ball on the tee. Give each child 5 completely free swings. Zero coaching. Watch what they naturally do. If the grip is dangerous (hands crossed): correct for safety. For everything else: let them swing. After 5 free swings: one cue maximum. Most common best cue at this age: "Swing with two hands together."
cue: Swing with two hands. Together!
why: Young kids learn a lot by just swinging. One cue at a time keeps it simple so they are not buried in instructions.
watch: Coaching more than one thing. Correcting things that do not matter yet.
harder: Move the tee to different spots. Try a slightly smaller ball.
easier: Lower the tee height. Let child hold the bat with both hands and just push the ball off first.

title: Run the Bases
setup: All players line up at home plate.
how: All players line up at home plate. On "go": first player runs to first base, touches it, continues to second, third, and home. Coach points and calls each base loudly: "First! Second! Third! Home!" Celebrate every player who completes the circuit. Run it again immediately. No rest. High enthusiasm from coach and teammates.
cue: Run to the base, not to me!
why: T-ball players need lots of trips around the bases to learn the order. Enthusiasm matters more than perfection at this stage.
watch: Players stopping at first out of habit. Running past home plate without touching it.
harder: Two players running simultaneously. Teaches not to run into each other.
easier: Coach walks alongside the player and points to each base while they run.

title: Bucket Toss
gear: Tennis balls, buckets or hula hoops
setup: Place buckets or hula hoops at various distances (5, 10, 15 feet). Players toss tennis balls trying to land in the targets.
how: Place buckets or hula hoops at 5 feet, 10 feet, and 15 feet. All players start at 5 feet. Each player throws 5 tennis balls underhand into the bucket. Make 3 in a row: move to 10 feet. Make 3 in a row: move to 15 feet. Count how far each player gets. No technique coaching. Just throw at the target.
cue: Throw it INTO the bucket. Not AT the bucket.
why: A clear target helps young kids learn direction and how hard to throw. Technique can come later; first they need to enjoy throwing.
watch: Players frustrating themselves. Keep the closest bucket easy enough for success.
harder: Overhand throw instead of underhand at 10 feet.
easier: 6-inch toss into a laundry basket at 3 feet.

title: Movement Circuit
gear: Cones, agility dots or chalk circles
setup: 5 stations in a circle: hop on one foot, broad jump, zigzag cones, roll and get up, balance on one foot for 5 seconds.
how: 5 stations arranged in a circle. Station 1: hop on one foot 10 times. Station 2: broad jump forward and back 5 times. Station 3: zigzag through 4 cones. Station 4: roll on the ground and jump up. Station 5: balance on one foot for 5 counts. Coach blows whistle every 45 seconds. Players rotate. Two full rotations. Make each station a game: "How many hops before the whistle?"
cue: Move like a baseball player. Quick feet, stay low!
why: Lots of different movements build general coordination at an age when kids are learning to control their bodies. It is also just fun.
watch: Players rushing through stations without engaging.
harder: Add a bat or ball at each station for sport-specific feel.
easier: Fewer stations (3). Coach at each station demonstrating.

title: Scatter Ball
setup: Scatter 8-10 foam balls in the infield. One team is fielders, one team is runners at home.
how: Scatter 8-10 foam balls across the infield. One team is runners at home, one team is fielders spread in the infield. On "go": runners try to pick up foam balls and put them in a central bucket. Fielders try to take foam balls away and hold them. No throwing. Carry only. After 60 seconds: count balls in the bucket. Switch teams. Celebrate the winner loudly.
cue: Get the ball, run it back. As fast as you can!
why: Chaos game that teaches spatial awareness and competitive engagement without requiring coordination skills they don't have yet.
watch: Throwing instead of carrying. Enforce the carry rule for safety.
harder: Add two buckets. Each team has their own bucket to fill.
easier: No competition. Just scatter and collect together as a team.

title: Live Scrimmage: Full Rules
setup: Full teams. Regular game rules. Coach keeps score and calls close plays.
how: Two full teams. Regular rules. Coach pitches or player pitches. Keep real score. Between innings: coach makes exactly ONE observation for each team. 30 seconds max. Players run on and off the field. Three or four complete innings. No stopping for instruction during the inning. Play it out. Debrief after all innings are complete.
cue: Play the game. Figure it out.
why: Kids make their own decisions in a real game. Holding coaching to between innings keeps the game moving and lets them figure things out.
watch: Coach over-coaching during play. Hold to the between-innings rule.
harder: Player pitching. Add consequence: winning team picks the next drill.
easier: Two innings only. Coach pitch.

title: Infield-Outfield Routine
setup: Full infield and outfield. Coach with fungo at home plate.
how: Standard pregame routine (sequences vary by team). Outfield: throws to second, then third, then home through the cutoff. Infield: coach hits grounders to each infielder, throw to first, then around the horn. Timed: complete the whole routine in 8 minutes. Run it once a week during practice so it feels familiar on game day.
cue: Pre-game routine. Own it.
why: Infield-outfield is a pregame ritual. Practicing it means kids know where to go on game day and it runs clean.
watch: Players not getting in position quickly enough. Cutoff not giving a target.
harder: Time the routine and try to beat the record.
easier: Run one position at a time before combining into the full routine.

title: Cutoffs and Relays
setup: Ball in the outfield. Relay players set up at standard positions. Infield holds.
how: Ball in the outfield. Relay player positions halfway between outfielder and the target base. Outfielder throws. Catcher or third baseman calls: "Cut third," "Cut home," or "Let it go." Relay player executes the call. 10 relays from each outfield position. After every 3 relays: ask the relay player "what are you listening for?"
cue: Relay: get in line between outfielder and the target. Give them a target with both arms up.
why: Cutoffs and relays are hard for young teams. Walking through it and then running it live gives kids a picture of where to be. The arms-up target helps the outfielder find the relay.
watch: Relay player not getting in line. Not giving target with both arms up.
harder: Live runners creating real time pressure.
easier: Walk through without a ball: relay player positions, makes the cut, simulates the redirect throw.

title: First and Third Situations
setup: Runners at first and third. Pitcher and full infield. No outfield needed.
how: Full infield. Runners at first and third. Coach pitches. Before each pitch: defense makes a call (which play they are running). On the pitch: offense executes their strategy. Defense executes their call. If defense executes correctly: they score a point. If offense scores the runner from third: offense scores. Play 8-10 live situations.
cue: Defense: make a call before the pitch and commit to it.
why: First and third can be confusing for young players. Running it live, with a call before each pitch, helps it make sense.
watch: Defense not making a call before the pitch.
harder: Add a full lineup. Hitters can help the offensive strategy.
easier: Walk through without pitching: show each defensive scenario before making it live.

title: Tee Work: One Location
setup: Set up a tee at belt height, slightly in front of your stride foot. Put a ball on it. Stand in your stance.
how: Set tee at belt height, just in front of the stride foot. Stand in your stance. Take 10 swings with one focus only. Watch where the ball goes after contact. That tells you more than any coach. After 10: adjust the tee one inch and notice if contact changes. 20 swings total per session.
cue: Drive through the ball. Not at it.
why: The tee is a simple, cheap way to get a lot of swings. The ball holds still, so the hitter can focus on one thing at a time.
watch: Changing your focus every swing. Swinging without a clear target for the ball.
harder: Move to two locations alternating. Record yourself on your phone and check hand position at contact.
easier: Slow-motion swings. Feel each position. Load, stride, contact, finish.

title: Tee Work: Two Locations
setup: Set up your tee. Call out "inside" or "outside" before each swing and move the tee accordingly. Inside = tee forward and in toward you. Outside = tee back and away.
how: Set tee at the inside spot: 10 swings. Reset to the outside spot: 10 swings. Now alternate by calling the location out loud before each swing and moving the tee. 20 alternating swings. Check: inside ball hit out front, outside ball allowed to travel deeper.
cue: Inside: pull it early. Outside: stay back.
why: You adjust your contact point every rep instead of grooving one spot. If the mix feels too hard, master one location first.
watch: Hitting both locations at the same contact point. Pulling the outside pitch.
harder: Add high and low as another variable. Randomize without calling: just move the tee and swing.
easier: One height per session. Master one before adding the other.

title: Self-Flip Soft Toss
gear: Wiffle ball or tennis ball, bat
setup: Stand in your batting stance holding the bat in your bottom hand. Hold a wiffle ball or tennis ball in your top hand.
how: Stand in batting stance, bat in your bottom hand, ball in your top hand. Flip the ball straight up 18-24 inches. Get both hands on the bat and let the ball drop into your contact zone. Swing through it. Hit into a net or an open field. 20 swings. Focus: wait for the ball to drop into your zone.
cue: Wait for it to drop into your zone.
why: A solo way to work on timing and waiting for the ball. No partner needed.
watch: Rushing the swing before the ball drops. Flipping the ball out in front instead of straight up.
harder: Try a sock ball for a different feel. Add a target zone marked with tape on a net.
easier: Even shorter toss. Just 6-8 inches. Slow motion first.

title: Bounce and Hit
gear: Rubber ball, bat, net or fence
setup: Stand 10-15 feet from a net or chain-link fence (not a solid wall, so the ball does not come flying back at you).
how: Stand 10-15 feet from a net or chain-link fence. Bat in the bottom hand, ball in the top hand. Drop the ball so it bounces about 2 feet in front of you and rises toward waist height. Get both hands on the bat and swing through it into the net. 20 reps.
cue: Let it come up to you. Swing when it reaches your zone.
why: A solo timing drill. The bounce gives a moving ball at different heights, a change of pace from the tee.
watch: Ball bouncing too close: drop it a little farther out. Swinging before the ball rises to the contact point. Never hit into a solid wall at close range.
harder: Drop from higher for a faster rise. Drop at an angle for a moving target.
easier: Shorter bounce. Let it die down to a slower speed first.

title: Tire Swings
setup: Hang an old tire or put a heavy bag at waist height. Stand in your stance and swing through it.
how: Stand in batting stance facing a tire or heavy bag hung at waist height. Swing through it with your regular bat, 20-30 swings with rest after every 10. Focus on finishing your swing through contact. Stop if hands, wrists, or elbows hurt.
cue: Finish your swing every rep. No half swings.
why: Hitting something solid gives feedback on whether you drive through contact or stop short. Keep the volume modest. The goal is feel, not a workout.
watch: Stopping the swing at contact. Sore hands or wrists: stop for the day.
harder: Swing from one knee to feel the turn. Alternate 5 tire swings with 5 tee swings.
easier: Shadow swings with no resistance first. Focus on follow-through before adding resistance.

title: Mirror Stance and Load Check
setup: Set up a mirror or prop your phone on video mode. Stand in your batting stance so you can see yourself from the front or side.
how: Prop your phone on video mode at knee height facing you from the front, or stand in front of a mirror. Take 10 slow-motion swings. After each, watch the replay or check the mirror. Pick ONE thing to look at per session: heel lift, hip rotation, hand path, or finish position. Never try to check more than one thing.
cue: See yourself before you fix yourself.
why: Seeing yourself gives feedback you cannot feel. A mirror or phone gives you that when no coach is around.
watch: Checking too many things at once. Moving the camera instead of positioning it well from the start.
harder: Record from the side as well to see bat path. Compare to a swing you admire from a video.
easier: No video. Just slow-motion swings with conscious body awareness.

title: Wall Ball: Grounders
setup: Stand 10-15 feet from a flat wall. Throw a tennis ball hard at the base of the wall so it comes back as a sharp grounder.
how: Stand 10-15 feet from a flat wall. Throw a tennis ball hard at the base of the wall so it bounces back as a sharp grounder. Field it. Vary throws: straight at you, angled left, angled right, short hop off the wall. 20 reps no-glove first. Then add glove. Progress: throw harder, get closer (8 feet) for faster returns.
cue: Get your body in front of it. Glove down, eyes up.
why: The wall sends the ball back fast, so you get lots of reps in a short time. Uneven walls add funny hops, which keeps you honest.
watch: Standing too far back. Move closer to create a more demanding return. Not getting in front of angled returns.
harder: Move to 8 feet for faster hops. Use a reaction ball against the wall.
easier: Underhand throw against the wall only. Slower speed.

title: Wall Ball: Pop-Ups
setup: Stand 15-20 feet from a wall. Throw the ball high against the wall so it comes off as a pop-up.
how: Stand 15-20 feet from a wall. Throw the ball high against the wall. Aim for a spot 8-10 feet up the wall. Read the rebound coming off as a pop-up. Move your feet first, then catch. 20 reps. Vary your throw angle to create pop-ups to your left, right, and directly above you.
cue: Find the ball early. Move your feet before you reach.
why: Fly ball reads are hard to practice alone. The wall gives you lots of pop-ups in a few minutes with just a tennis ball.
watch: Reaching for pop-ups instead of moving feet first. Camping directly under it without room to adjust.
harder: Throw against two walls at a corner for a more unpredictable rebound.
easier: Shorter throw at 6 feet up the wall for a slower, more predictable pop-up.

title: Bare-Hand Wall Drill
setup: Stand 8 feet from a wall. No glove. Throw a tennis ball at the wall and field the rebound with bare hands.
how: Stand 8 feet from a wall. No glove. Throw tennis ball against the wall and field the rebound bare-handed. The key: hands receive the ball. Don't grab at it. Feel the ball land and give backward slightly. 20 reps. Then put glove on and take 10 more reps. The glove should feel forgiving after bare hands.
cue: Soft hands. Let the ball come to you.
why: Taking the glove off makes you feel whether you are receiving the ball or grabbing at it. Then the glove feels easy.
watch: Flinching away from the ball. One-handed attempts.
harder: Move to 6 feet. Throw harder.
easier: Bounce ball off the floor instead of the wall for a slower, predictable return.

title: Bucket Grounder Drill
setup: Bucket of 10-15 balls next to you. Open space in front of you. An empty bucket or fence 20 feet away as a throwing target (optional).
how: Bucket of balls next to you. Roll or toss one ball 10-20 feet out ahead of you. Get into ready position as it rolls, then charge and field it with the glove down and two hands. Return it to the bucket. 25 reps. Focus: glove down early, two hands on every ball, clean transfer after fielding.
cue: Two hands. Always two hands.
why: Simple, high-rep solo work. Good for beginners building the basic fielding habit before adding speed.
watch: One-handed fields. Glove late. Must be down before the ball arrives.
harder: Roll faster. Roll to different sides.
easier: Start with the ball already on the ground in front of you. Just pick it up with correct two-hand technique.

title: Tennis Racket Fly Balls
setup: Stand in outfield or large open area. Hold a glove in one hand, tennis racket in the other. Drop a tennis ball and hit it straight up.
how: Hold glove in one hand, tennis racket in the other. Drop a tennis ball in front of you and hit it straight up with the racket. Track it and catch with the glove. 15 catches. Then hit the ball with deliberate spin to the left. Run to it and catch. Then spin to the right. The racket adds a little spin, so the ball does not always go where you expect.
cue: Move first. Then catch. Don't stand and wait.
why: Fly balls are hard to practice alone. A racket gets the ball up high, and the spin makes it move a little, which keeps you tracking.
watch: Swinging too hard. The ball goes too high and too far. Not tracking early enough.
harder: Hit behind yourself and run to track it down.
easier: Just toss straight up with your bare hand and catch in the glove. No racket yet.

title: Toss and Catch to Yourself
setup: Stand in an open area. Toss the ball straight up with your bare hand and catch it in your glove.
how: Toss a baseball or tennis ball straight up with your bare hand. Catch it in your glove. Start at 6-8 feet high. Work up to 15-20 feet. 20 catches. Then: toss slightly to your left and right. Must move feet before catching. Rule: fingers up for balls above the waist, fingers down for balls below. Check this on every catch.
cue: Fingers up above the waist, fingers down below.
why: The easiest solo catching drill there is. All you need is a ball and a glove. Great for young players getting their first reps.
watch: Fingers in wrong position. Not moving feet. Just reaching.
harder: Toss 5-10 feet to the side and sprint to it.
easier: Just toss 4 feet high and catch. Very low, slow, easy.

title: Wall Target Throwing
setup: Put three pieces of tape on a wall: one at knee height, one chest height, one shoulder height. Stand 20 feet away.
how: Put three tape targets on a wall: knee, chest, shoulder. Stand 20 feet away. Call the target out loud before each throw. 5 throws per target. Move to 30 feet and repeat. Move to 40 feet. Track your hit rate at each distance. Compete against your last session's score.
cue: Pick a spot. Throw to a spot, not at the wall.
why: Calling a target gives you something to aim at and a score to beat. Good reps without a partner.
watch: Not calling target before throwing. Throwing without a follow-through.
harder: Add a fourth target in a corner. Require the throw within 5 seconds of calling.
easier: Larger targets. Shorter distance (15 feet).

title: Field and Fire at the Fence
setup: Mark a chest-high target on a chain-link fence or backstop (a towel or tape square). Stand 30-45 feet away with a few balls.
how: Mark a chest-high target on a fence or backstop. Stand 30-45 feet away. Roll a ball out, charge it, field it, set your feet, and throw to the target. Hit = 1 point. After 5 throws, walk up and collect the balls. 20 throws total at comfortable effort, never max effort. Stop if your arm is sore.
cue: Field it, find the target, throw.
why: Combines fielding and throwing at a target, the way it happens in a game. The target gives instant feedback. Keep the throw count modest and the effort comfortable.
watch: Throwing max effort. Rushing the throw before finding the target. Any arm pain: stop and tell a parent.
harder: Roll the ball to your glove side and backhand side. Time yourself from field to throw.
easier: Stay at 20-30 feet. Tennis balls. Skip the ground ball and just throw at the target.

title: Wall Catch Streak
setup: Stand 12-15 feet from a flat wall with a tape target at chest height.
how: Stand 12-15 feet from a wall with a tape target at chest height. Easy throws at the tape. Catch the rebound with two hands. Count your streak of clean catches. A miss or a chase resets to zero. 20-30 throws at comfortable effort.
cue: Hit the tape. Catch it clean.
why: A simple solo game: aim at a target and catch what comes back. Counting streaks keeps it fun and keeps attention on the target and the catch.
watch: Throwing hard so the rebound gets wild. One-handed stabs.
harder: Step back to 20 feet. Move the target lower so rebounds come back as short hops.
easier: Stand closer (8 feet). Underhand throws.

title: Bucket Target Throws
setup: Place a bucket or large trash can 15 feet away. Step back to 20 feet after making 3 in a row.
how: Bucket 15 feet away. Throw 5 tennis balls in. Count makes. Move to 20 feet after 3 consecutive makes. Then 25, 30, 35 feet. Track your max distance where you can make 3 in a row. At longer distances: throw with an arc, not flat. Compete: can you beat last week's max distance?
cue: High arc from far away. Low line drive from close.
why: A bucket is an easy target to aim at, and beating your own score is built-in motivation.
watch: Flat throws on longer distances. They miss short.
harder: Smaller target (coffee can) at short distances.
easier: Underhand toss at 8 feet with a laundry basket.

title: Jump Rope
setup: Any flat surface. No setup beyond the rope.
how: 3 rounds: 1 minute jumping, 30 seconds rest. Week 1: basic two-foot jumps. Week 2: alternate feet. Left, right, left, right. Week 3: double-unders if able (rope goes under twice per jump). Track your longest consecutive streak without tripping each session. Post it and try to beat it.
cue: Light on your feet. Like you're ready to react.
why: A cheap, fun way to build foot speed, rhythm, and coordination. Kids can track streaks and try to beat them.
watch: Jumping too high: stay low and quick. During growth spurts, cut the rounds and skip double-unders if knees or heels are sore.
harder: Double-unders. Alternate-foot sprint rhythm.
easier: Just 30-second sets. Basic two-foot jumps only.

title: Lateral Shuffle Cone Drill
setup: Place 2 cones 10 feet apart. Start at one cone in an athletic stance: knees bent, weight forward, feet shoulder-width.
how: Place 2 cones 10 feet apart. Athletic stance: knees bent, weight forward, feet shoulder-width. Shuffle to one cone, touch it with outside hand, shuffle back. Repeat: 10 reps = one set. Three sets. Key: stay low throughout. Do not stand up while shuffling. Progress: add a W-pattern with a third cone in the middle.
cue: Stay low the whole time. Don't stand up as you move.
why: Side-to-side movement shows up all over baseball: fielding, baserunning, backing up plays. Quick, free, and easy to do anywhere.
watch: Standing up between shuffles. Crossing feet. Feet never cross in a shuffle.
harder: W-pattern. Time yourself.
easier: Slow walk-speed shuffle. Focus on foot position.

title: Standing Broad Jump Series
setup: Mark a starting line with tape or chalk. Stand at the line with feet shoulder-width.
how: Mark a starting line. Stand with feet shoulder-width. Swing arms back, bend knees, then drive arms forward and jump as far as possible. Land softly on both feet. Controlled landing, no falling forward. Mark where you land. 5 jumps. Rest 60 seconds. 3 sets. Track your best jump distance each session.
cue: Explode out and up. Stick the landing.
why: A simple bodyweight jump that builds leg power and good landings. Tracking your best jump is fun and shows progress.
watch: Landing without control, collapsing forward. No arm drive. During growth spurts, cut to 1-2 sets and stop if knees or heels are sore.
harder: Broad jump into a short sprint. Single-leg broad jumps for older, experienced players only.
easier: Step broad jump. Step forward with one foot then push off for the jump.

title: Single-Leg Balance Work
setup: Stand barefoot on a flat surface. This drill requires no equipment.
how: Stand on one foot for 30 seconds. Then eyes closed. Much harder. 3 holds per foot. Progress: balance on one foot and toss a tennis ball to yourself. The toss and catch challenge forces the body to stabilize dynamically.
cue: Find one point on the ground. Stare at it.
why: Balance helps with fielding, running, and hitting. Balance work is part of many injury-prevention warm-ups used in youth sports, and it is cheap and safe.
watch: Body swaying wildly. Find a single focal point on the ground to stare at.
harder: Balance on one foot and swing the other leg forward and back while staying stable.
easier: Eyes open only. Hold for 15 seconds.

title: Baseball Plank Series
setup: Any flat surface. Three positions: front plank, left side plank, right side plank.
how: Three positions in sequence: (1) Front plank. Elbows under shoulders, straight line head to heel, 30 seconds. (2) Left side plank. Bottom elbow under shoulder, body straight, 20 seconds. (3) Right side plank. Same, 20 seconds. Rest 30 seconds. Repeat twice. Progress: in each position, add a reach or leg lift for 5 reps.
cue: Straight line from head to heel. Squeeze everything.
why: A bodyweight way to build trunk strength with no equipment. Good general fitness for any athlete, and easy to do at home.
watch: Hips sagging in front plank. Side plank body rotating forward.
harder: Plank with alternating arm reach. Add 5-second holds at each position.
easier: Plank from knees rather than full position.

title: Agility Ladder Patterns
gear: Agility ladder or chalk on pavement
setup: Lay out the ladder on flat ground. No ladder: draw 10 squares with chalk, each about 18 inches across.
how: Lay ladder on flat ground. Pattern 1: one foot in each box, fast. Pattern 2: two feet in each box. Pattern 3: in-in-out-out (Ickey Shuffle). 3 runs through per pattern. 30-second rest between patterns. Track: time each run through. Look forward. Not down at the ladder. Arms pump like sprinting.
cue: Look forward. Not down at the ladder.
why: Fun footwork patterns that build coordination and rhythm. How much ladder work carries over to game quickness is unclear, so treat it as a good warm-up, not a magic fix.
watch: Looking down at the ladder. Eyes forward.
harder: Add a sprint for 10 yards after exiting the ladder.
easier: Walk speed only. Two patterns max.

title: Pitch Count and Rest Log
setup: Keep a simple log for every day you pitch: the date, pitches thrown, and how your arm felt (1-5).
how: Every day you pitch, log: date, pitches thrown (games plus bullpens), and arm feel from 1 to 5. Before the next outing, check the log against your league's rest-day rules. Also note if you caught or pitched for another team that week. Any pain, not just normal tiredness: stop throwing and tell a parent.
cue: Count every pitch. Rest is part of the plan.
why: Pitch counts and rest days are the most widely recommended way to protect young arms (Pitch Smart, Little League rules). A log makes the count visible to everyone.
watch: Forgetting bullpens and second teams. Pitching and catching on the same day. Pitching through pain.
harder: Add weekly and season totals. Plan a real break from competitive pitching each year, as Pitch Smart recommends.
easier: Just the date and pitch count. Add arm feel later.

title: Solo Stork Balance
setup: Stand on flat ground. No ball needed.
how: Stand on one leg, other knee lifted toward hip height. Hold 10-20 seconds without touching down. 5 holds per leg. Then try it with eyes closed, or while tossing a tennis ball to yourself. Keep a record of your longest hold.
cue: Pick a spot, stay tall, stay still.
why: Balance is a general athletic skill for everyone, pitchers included. This is a balance challenge, not a delivery lesson. Delivery coaching belongs with a qualified pitching coach.
watch: Holding your breath. Locking the standing knee straight: keep a soft bend.
harder: Eyes closed. Catch a self-toss while balancing. Stand on a folded towel.
easier: Fingertips on a wall. Hold 5 seconds.

title: Net Spot Work
setup: Set up a net with a strike zone target at proper pitching distance (46 feet for Little League, 60.5 feet for high school). Aim at 4 quadrants: up-in, up-out, down-in, down-out.
how: Net with target at 46 feet (Little League). Call target zone out loud before every pitch: "Down and away." Throw. Mark hit or miss on a scorecard. 20 pitches. Track which zone you miss most. Spend 5 extra pitches on your weakest zone at the end of every session. Keep the scorecard.
cue: See the corner. Throw to the corner.
why: A target and a scorecard turn solo throwing into a game, and charting shows where your misses go. Count these pitches toward your daily limit.
watch: Not calling the target before throwing. Throwing to the same zone every time. Any arm pain: stop for the day.
harder: Add a batter standing (not swinging) in the box for visual context.
easier: Shorter distance (35 feet). Larger target zone.

title: At-Bat Visualization
setup: Sit or lie down in a quiet space. Eyes closed.
how: Sit or lie down quietly. Eyes closed. Five full at-bats in your mind. Each one: see the pitcher, see the ball leave their hand, see it travel, see your swing, see where the ball goes. Make them vivid. Feel the bat, hear the crack, sense the pressure of the moment. After: say out loud what you saw in at-bat 3.
cue: See it perfectly before you try it.
why: Imagery is a common sport psychology tool with some research support, mostly in older athletes. Treat it as mental reps: short, vivid, and specific. It does not replace real swings.
watch: Mind wandering. If you lose focus, start that at-bat over.
harder: Visualize yourself in the most stressful situation you have ever faced. See yourself succeeding.
easier: Just one at-bat. Just the pitch coming in and making contact.

title: One-Thing Practice Journal
setup: After every solo session or game, write or type one sentence.
how: After every session or game: write or type one sentence starting with "Today I improved my ___." Not a list. One thing. Date every entry. After 30 entries: look back at the first 10. Are the same things showing up? If yes: it became a strength. If no: you improved many areas. Both are wins.
cue: One thing. Not a list. Find the win.
why: Writing down one improvement helps players notice progress they would otherwise miss. Looking back later shows what keeps getting better.
watch: Writing lists instead of one thing. Skipping sessions. Habit only works with consistency.
harder: Add a second sentence: "Tomorrow I want to work on ___."
easier: Voice memo instead of writing.

title: Color Tag
setup: Place 4 colored cones at corners of a 30x30 boundary. Two players are taggers, everyone else is free.
how: Place cones before players arrive. Two players start as taggers inside the boundary. Coach stands outside and calls a color every 15-20 seconds. Everyone sprints to that cone. Last player to touch it joins the taggers. If tagged mid-run: also joins the taggers. Run until 3-4 players remain free, then reset. 4 rounds.
cue: Listen. Then explode. Don't move before you hear the color.
why: Kids have to hear the color, think, and then go. Lots of quick starts, and it keeps everyone listening.
watch: Players pre-moving before the color is called. Call it out. Taggers giving up. Swap them out after each round.
harder: Call two colors at once. Players pick one. Call colors faster with less warning.
easier: Walk only. No tagging. Just racing to the cone.

title: Mirror Partner Drill
setup: Partners face each other 4 feet apart. One leads, one mirrors every movement.
how: Partners face each other 4 feet apart. Designate leader and mirror. Leader makes lateral shuffles, forward/backward steps, arm raises, squats. Anything athletic. Mirror matches every movement as fast as possible. 45 seconds leading, switch. Three rounds each. Final round: no designated leader. Both react simultaneously.
cue: React. Don't predict.
why: Kids react to a partner they cannot predict, so it is quick-feet practice with a game feel. No equipment needed.
watch: Leaders making non-athletic movements (jumping jacks, etc.). Redirect to baseball movements: shuffle, ready position, load. Mirrors looking at feet instead of their partner.
harder: Leader can use diagonal movements and pivots. Add a ball. Leader holds ball and randomly offers it; mirror must react to take or block.
easier: Slow-motion only. Leader calls the movement before doing it.

title: Tail Tag Infield Race
setup: Split players into pairs. Each player tucks a pinnie in their waistband as a tail. Set a 30x30 boundary with cones.
how: Pair players before starting. Each player tucks a pinnie 12 inches out of their waistband. On "go," each player in the pair tries to steal their partner's tail. First to steal it wins the pair. Immediately announce new matchups. Rotate so players face different opponents. After 5 rounds: survivor bracket, last tail standing wins.
cue: Stay low. Change direction with short steps, not big ones.
why: Short one-on-one battles keep intensity high and everyone moving at once.
watch: Grabbing clothing. Players running out of boundary. Call them back.
harder: Three-player triangles instead of pairs. Winner of each pair must face each other in a final.
easier: Partners must stay within 10 feet of each other at all times.

title: Rock Paper Scissors Sprint
gear: Two cones or bases 20 feet apart
setup: Two teams on opposite lines facing each other, 20 feet apart.
how: One player from each team walks to the center line. They face each other and play rock-paper-scissors simultaneously. Three counts, reveal. Winner immediately sprints back to their team's safety base. Loser chases and tries to tag before they arrive. No tag = winner scores a point. Tagged = no point. Rotate through all players. First team to 10 wins.
cue: Explode off your back foot the second you win!
why: Nobody knows who will sprint until the reveal, so kids react instead of anticipating. Kids love it, and it gives lots of quick starts.
