watch: False starts before the reveal. Taggers giving up early. Remind them it counts.
harder: Winner must sprint around a cone before reaching safety. Loser gets a 1-second head start.
easier: No chasing. Just race to see who gets to the cone first.

title: Hula Hoop Relay
setup: Scatter hula hoops across the field. Two teams start at opposite ends.
how: Set up 4-5 hoops in a line as a course. Two teams race simultaneously on parallel courses. Players must step into each hoop with both feet before moving to the next. At the end: run back and tag the next player. First team to get all players through wins. Run 3 races.
cue: Quick feet through the hoop. Don't slow down!
why: The hoops show young kids exactly where to step without much talking. Relays add energy and teamwork.
watch: Players skipping hoops. Tagging before the previous player is back.
harder: Balance on one foot inside each hoop for 2 seconds.
easier: One foot in each hoop only. No stopping required.

title: Dynamic Stretch Circuit
setup: Players line up at one end of a 30-yard lane. Each movement goes down and back.
how: Players line up single file at one end. Call each movement: (1) High knees. Drive knees to hip height, arms pumping, down the line. (2) Butt kicks. Heels to glutes, back the line. (3) Walking lunges with torso rotation. Step forward, lunge, rotate opposite elbow to front knee. (4) Lateral shuffle. Face the sideline, stay low, shuffle the width. (5) Inchworm. Hands to ground, walk out to push-up position, one push-up, walk back up. (6) High skip. Big arm swing, exaggerated skip, maximum height. Two full circuits.
cue: Move through the range. Don't hold it.
why: Moving warm-ups raise body temperature and rehearse the movements kids are about to use. No long static holds, and the line keeps moving.
watch: Players bouncing during lateral shuffles. Stay low. Inchworm without the push-up. High knees not reaching hip height. Cue "drive your knee up."
harder: Add a 5-yard acceleration sprint at the end of each movement. Increase the lunge rotation range.
easier: Walk pace only. Skip the inchworm for very young players.

title: Short Hop Gauntlet
setup: Partners 12-15 feet apart. One player is the short-hopper. They throw intentionally short so the ball bounces once before reaching the fielder.
how: Partners face each other 12 feet apart. Short-hopper throws intentionally short so the ball must bounce once before reaching the fielder. Fielder must attack the hop. Move forward slightly to meet it, rather than waiting. 15 reps glove-side, 15 reps backhand. After each set, switch roles. Compete: how many clean fields out of 15?
cue: Attack the hop. Don't wait for it to come to you.
why: Short hops are tough for young fielders and do not come up much in regular grounder lines. Moving forward to take the hop gives them a plan.
watch: Fielder backing up on the hop. They must step into it. Throwing too hard. The hop should be playable. Backhand technique: glove elbow leads.
harder: Increase distance to 15 feet so the hop has more speed. Mix glove-side and backhand randomly.
easier: Use a tennis ball off a wall instead of a partner throw. Distance of 8 feet only.

title: Rapid Fire Grounders
setup: Coach with 10 tennis balls in a bucket, 25 feet from fielder. Fielder in ready position.
how: Fielder in ready position 25 feet away. Coach has 10 balls in bucket. Coach rolls grounder 1. Fielder fields and tosses aside. Coach immediately rolls grounder 2 without pause. Continue through all 10. Fielder must reset to ready position between each ball. Rest 45 seconds. Three sets. Track clean fields per set.
cue: Reset fast. Don't watch where the last one went.
why: Quick reps force a fast reset after each ball, like after a play in a game. Lots of touches in a few minutes.
watch: Fielder watching the previous ball after fielding it. Not getting back to ready position before the next roll. Coach: keep the pace up. 3-4 seconds maximum between rolls.
harder: Mix in pop-ups every 3rd ball. Random directions instead of straight at the fielder. Reduce rest to 30 seconds.
easier: 5-ball sets instead of 10. 6-second gaps between rolls.

title: No-Glove Scoop Drill
setup: Partners 15 feet apart, NO gloves. One rolls grounders, one fields bare-handed.
how: Partners 15 feet apart, both without gloves. One rolls a grounder, the other fields bare-handed. Field with two hands. Glove-hand side underneath to receive the ball, throwing hand on top to trap and secure it. 20 reps. Then both put gloves on. Take 10 more reps and compare the feel of your hands. The bare-hand softness should carry over.
cue: Two hands. Soft and give with the ball.
why: Taking the glove away makes soft, two-hand fielding the only way to catch the ball. The constraint does the teaching with very few words.
watch: One-handed attempts. Players flinching away from the ball. Use tennis balls if needed. Hands going stiff on contact.
harder: Roll faster. Add a throw to a target after each field. Progress to irregular-bounce reaction ball.
easier: Tennis balls only. Very slow rolls. Player fields from kneeling position first.

title: Reaction Ball Grounders
setup: Partners 12 feet apart. One player drops and bounces a reaction ball. Its irregular shape creates unpredictable bounces.
how: Partners 12 feet apart. One player drops the reaction ball from waist height. Does not throw it. Let it bounce. Fielder reads the unpredictable direction and fields it. 20 drops. Switch. Then one player throws the reaction ball underhand at the wall. Fielder reads the rebound. Compare to regular ball after each set.
cue: Stay low and ready. You can't predict it, so stay athletic.
why: The odd bounces mean nobody can guess where the ball is going, so fielders stay low and react. Kids tend to find it fun and challenging.
watch: Fielder trying to predict the bounce direction instead of reacting. Standing too upright. Reinforce the athletic ready position.
harder: Increase to 15 feet. Throw against wall instead of drop. Mix with regular ball randomly.
easier: Drop only (no throw). Fielder starts closer and the partner drops from a lower height.

title: Dive and Recover
gear: Tennis balls, soft grass or turf area, gloves
setup: Outfield grass. Fielder starts standing. Partner stands 10 feet away with a bucket of tennis balls.
how: Fielder starts in ready position on soft outfield grass or turf ONLY. Never run this drill on dirt, gravel, or hard infield surfaces. Partner stands 10 feet away with bucket of tennis balls. Partner tosses a ball far to the right or left. Outside arm's reach. Fielder dives to reach it. Land on the forearm. Not the elbow. Glove stays in front. Pop up immediately after catching. Reset. 10 dives each direction. Emphasize: dive through the ball, not at it.
cue: Dive through the ball. Keep your glove in front as you land.
why: Diving is part of the game, and kids who practice it on soft grass learn to land safely. Keep it on grass or turf and keep reps low.
watch: Landing on the elbow. Correct immediately for safety. Fielder diving early before reading the toss direction. Not popping up after. They must recover immediately.
harder: Partner calls the direction right before tossing. Reduces the read time. Mix in balls the fielder can reach without diving.
easier: Low foam balls only. Softer ground or tumbling mat. Start with a step-and-reach instead of a full dive.

title: Triangle Cutoff Drill
setup: Ball in left field. Shortstop as the cutoff for throws to third. Third baseman at the bag. Catcher at home.
how: Ball starts in left field. The cutoff lines up between the outfielder and the target base (one common system: shortstop cuts throws to third, third baseman cuts throws home from left field). Left fielder throws to the cutoff. The player at the target base calls "cut" or "let it go." Cutoff executes the call. Run 5 reps from left field. Then 5 from right field with the shortstop cutting throws to third. Debrief: who makes the call and why?
cue: Cutoff: face the outfielder, not the target. Turn to redirect.
why: Cutoff alignment is hard for young players to picture. Doing it with real throws shows them where to stand and which way to turn.
watch: Cutoff man not getting in line between outfielder and target. Cutoff man facing the wrong way. No cut call being made.
harder: Add a live runner to create real time pressure. Mix in balls the cutoff should let go.
easier: No runners. Coach makes the cut call until fielders understand the concept.

title: Outfield Drop-Step Angles
gear: Fungo or soft toss, balls, gloves
setup: Outfielder in starting position. Coach with fungo or standing 10 feet away with balls.
how: Outfielder starts in ready position. Coach hits or soft-tosses 15 balls. Mix of: over the left shoulder, over the right shoulder, straight back, and shallow. On each ball: outfielder must drop-step in the correct direction BEFORE running. No backpedaling allowed. After each rep, ask: "Which direction was your first step?" Fielder answers.
cue: Drop step first. Then run. Never backpedal.
why: Many young outfielders backpedal on balls over their heads. The drop step gives them a simple first move, and it takes repetition before it shows up in games.
watch: Any backpedaling. Stop the rep and restart with emphasis on the drop step. Fielder running before drop-stepping.
harder: Add communication with a second outfielder. Coach disguises the direction. Starts to hit one way then adjusts.
easier: Coach points in the direction before hitting. Fielder just practices the drop step footwork without a ball.

title: Charge and Field
setup: Fielder stands 30 feet from the coach. Coach rolls slow grounders that die 15-20 feet in front of fielder.
how: Fielder starts 30 feet from coach. Coach rolls a slow grounder that will stop 15-20 feet in front of the fielder. They must charge to meet it. Field it on the glove-side foot. Left foot for right-handed fielders. Barehand if the ball is dead. After fielding, simulate a throw to first. 15 reps. Then add a real throw to a player at first.
cue: Attack slow rollers. Field it on your glove-side foot.
why: Slow rollers are tough for young infielders, and many wait on them instead of charging. This gives lots of reps at attacking the ball.
watch: Fielder waiting for the ball instead of charging. Fielding off the wrong foot. Reinforces a weak throwing position. Hesitation on the barehand. It's fast, don't think.
harder: Add a real first baseman and time the throw. Fielder starts in ready position on one knee.
easier: Fielder starts only 20 feet away. Shorter charge distance. Slow tosses rather than rolls.

title: Wall Ball Competition
setup: Two players compete side-by-side at a wall. Each throws and fields their own ball. Boundary line between them.
how: Two players stand side by side at a wall, each with their own tennis ball. Boundary line between them on the floor. Both throw and field simultaneously. Each only fields their own ball. If a player misses a clean rebound, crosses the line, or their ball rolls away: opponent scores a point. First to 10 wins. Play 3 games.
cue: Quick hands. Field it clean and throw again.
why: Competition makes kids go hard, and wall ball gives tons of reps with just a ball and a wall.
watch: Players interfering with each other's balls. Not tracking their own ball after throwing.
harder: Speed it up. Throw immediately after fielding. Reduce the boundary line width.
easier: Take turns instead of simultaneous. One ball, pass it back and forth off the wall.

title: Second Base Double Play Feed
setup: Second baseman and shortstop at their positions. Fielder at first. Coach at home rolling grounders.
how: Coach rolls grounders from home. Shortstop fields, feeds to second baseman covering the bag. 2B catches, pivots, throws to first. Five reps SS feeds to 2B. Five reps 2B fields and SS covers. 2B feeds to SS who turns and throws to first. Key coaching point: feed to the chest, not the feet. Pivot player steps toward first on the catch. Add a runner after the first 5 reps.
cue: Feed to the chest. Never make the pivot player reach.
why: The double play turn has a lot of moving parts. A chest-high feed makes the pivot easier, so it is a good first habit to build.
watch: Low feeds forcing the pivot player to reach down. Corrects immediately. Pivot player turning the wrong direction. No urgency. They must treat every rep like a real out.
harder: Live runner on first. Bunt situations where the pitcher fields and feeds.
easier: No runner. Slow rollers only. Focus only on the feed. No turn or throw to first yet.

title: Opposite Field Drill
gear: Tee or soft toss, balls, net or field
setup: Tee set up on the outside corner (back of the plate, away from hitter). Cones mark the opposite-field zone.
how: Set tee on the outside corner. Back of the plate, away side. Mark the opposite-field landing zone with cones (right field for right-handed hitter). Hitter takes 15 swings. Ball must land in the opposite-field zone to count. Any pull-side hit = do-over immediately. Coaching emphasis: stay back, let the ball travel deep, drive it the other way.
cue: Let it get deep. Stay behind the ball.
why: Hitting the other way helps hitters cover the outside part of the plate. The cones give a clear target and instant feedback.
watch: Hitter pulling the outside pitch. Hips opening too early. Not staying back. Weight shifting forward too soon.
harder: Coach pitch outside location instead of tee. Add a "drive it in the gap" requirement. Not just any opposite field contact.
easier: Set tee in middle of plate first. Just work on staying back before adding the outside location.

title: Three-Pitch At-Bat
setup: Pitcher, catcher, one hitter. Only three pitches per at-bat, regardless of count.
how: Pitcher, catcher, one hitter. Three pitches. That's the at-bat regardless of count. Before the first pitch, hitter tells the catcher what pitch location they are looking for. After the third pitch, hitter explains their decisions out loud: "First pitch was outside, I took it. Second was in my zone, I swung. Third I guessed wrong." Coach listens, asks one follow-up question.
cue: Know what you're looking for before the pitch.
why: Having a plan before the pitch is a skill. Three pitches, then talk about it, gets hitters thinking about their decisions.
watch: Hitter not having a plan before the pitch. Swinging at pitches outside their stated zone.
harder: Pitcher pitches without any pre-stated target. Real game randomness. Add a runner on base for situational context.
easier: Two-pitch at-bat only. Hitter and pitcher agree on the pitch location before each one.

title: No-Stride Tee Drill
setup: Hitter in stance with feet already in the post-stride position. Front foot already planted forward.
how: Hitter sets up with front foot already planted in the post-stride position. Feet wider than normal stance. Hands back in load. On the pitch or tee: swing with no stride, only rotation. 20 swings. After: take 10 normal swings and feel how the rotation carries over. The goal is isolating hip rotation. Hitter should feel their back hip driving first.
cue: All rotation. Feel your hips lead your hands.
why: Taking the stride away removes a timing piece so the hitter can feel the turn. A simple way to check whether the hips are getting involved.
watch: Hitter still trying to stride. Front foot must stay planted. Weight not shifting from back to front during rotation.
harder: Add a resistance band around the hips to feel the rotation. Progress to a short stride after mastering no-stride.
easier: Swing in slow motion first. Exaggerate the hip-turn so the hitter can feel the movement.

title: Soft Toss Reaction
setup: Tosser kneels 10-12 feet to the side of the hitter with a bucket of balls.
how: Tosser kneels to the side 10-12 feet with a bucket of balls. Tosser randomly: (1) tosses normally, (2) fakes and holds the ball, or (3) tosses to a different height than usual. Hitter must only swing on real tosses at their zone. After 20 tosses, count: how many correct decisions? Swing on a fake or take on a real one = wrong.
cue: See it, decide, then swing. Never the other way.
why: Regular soft toss gets into a rhythm where kids swing because a toss is coming. Fakes and height changes make them decide each time.
watch: Hitter starting the swing before the ball is released. Guessing instead of reading. They should wait as long as possible.
harder: Add colored balls. Only swing at specific colors. Tosser moves to slightly different positions each toss.
easier: No fakes yet. Just alternate high and low tosses with a verbal call.

title: Inside-Out Swing Drill
setup: Tee set on inside corner (in front of plate, close to hitter). Place a cone or obstacle on the pull-side as a gate the bat must NOT go through.
how: Set tee on the inside corner. Forward and in. Place a cone or batting tee directly on the pull side as a gate. The bat barrel must pass inside the gate before reaching the contact point. Hitter swings 15 times focusing on "hands first, barrel follows." Any bat path that hits the gate = do-over. After 15 good reps: remove the gate and swing 10 more.
cue: Hands first. Barrel follows.
why: The gate gives a clear, visible check on the bat path. Kids know right away if the barrel went around.
watch: Bat going around the gate instead of inside it. Hitter muscling the ball with the arms instead of driving the barrel through.
harder: Use a second gate on the opposite side. Hitter must drive the ball to the opposite field through the narrow window.
easier: No gate yet. Just work on the inside-contact tee location with hands-first emphasis.

title: Game At-Bat Simulation
setup: Pitcher, catcher, hitter. Full count situation announced before each at-bat.
how: Coach announces before each pitch: "Runner on second. One out. 1-1 count." Pitcher and hitter play it out live. Real pitches, real decisions. After each at-bat: pause. Ask the hitter: "What was your job? Did you do it?" Ask the defender who made a play: "What did you read first?" Run 3 at-bats per hitter, 2 complete rotations through the lineup.
cue: What's your job in this situation. Before the pitch.
why: Knowing the situation before the pitch changes how a hitter approaches the at-bat. Playing it live gives real decisions, and the debrief connects the two.
watch: Hitter not adjusting approach to the situation. Defense not pre-setting before the pitch.
harder: Add live baserunners. Keep real score across all at-bats.
easier: Coach tells the hitter their job before each pitch: "Hit it to the right side."

title: Variable Speed Coach Pitch
setup: Coach pitches from 30-35 feet. Varies speed: slow lob, medium, slightly faster. Never warns the hitter which is coming.
how: Coach pitches from 30-35 feet. Three speeds without warning: (1) slow lob, (2) medium arc, (3) faster flat pitch. Never tell the hitter which is coming. Hitter gets 8 pitches per turn. No count. Just swing at strikes. After a hit, hitter runs to first. Rotate after every player has batted. Keep score. Team batting vs team fielding.
cue: Watch the ball come out of the hand. Not at the ball.
why: Real pitching changes speed. Mixing speeds makes hitters adjust their timing instead of settling into one rhythm.
watch: Hitter timing one speed and getting jammed by the faster one. Swinging at balls. Coach should challenge the zone but keep pitches hittable.
harder: Add a changeup. Exaggerated slow pitch after a faster one. Mix in intentional balls to force take decisions.
easier: Two speeds only. Announce slow or fast before each pitch until hitters are comfortable reading.

title: Color Ball Drill
gear: Balls marked with colored dots (red, blue), sharpie
setup: Mark baseballs: red dot on one side, blue dot on the other. Coach tosses from behind an L-screen. Hitter sees the ball spinning.
how: Mark baseballs with a red dot on one hemisphere and a blue dot on the other using a sharpie. Coach tosses from behind L-screen 15-20 feet away with a medium arc. Note: this drill requires enough velocity for the ball to spin visibly. Works best with live player pitching. Slow coach-pitch arcs may not spin fast enough for reliable color identification. As the ball leaves the hand, it spins and the hitter sees the rotating dots. Coach calls "red" or "blue" at the moment of release. Hitter swings only on the called color. 20 tosses.
cue: Read the spin. Your eyes are faster than you think.
why: A fun way to make hitters watch the ball closely. Some college programs use pitch-recognition training, but evidence at youth levels is thin. Treat it as a focus game.
watch: Hitter making decisions before the ball is in flight. Swinging at the wrong color. Enforce the discipline.
harder: Coach stops calling the color. Hitter reads and decides. Mix in a third color (no swing).
easier: Coach holds the ball up and shows the color before tossing. Hitter confirms the color before swinging.

title: Top-Hand Tee Drill
setup: Remove the bottom hand from the bat (or grip loosely). Swing 10 times using only the top hand.
how: Remove the bottom hand or grip loosely. Top hand only. 10 swings off the tee. Focus: one widely-taught approach: palm facing up or outward at the contact point, delaying wrist roll-over. Note: some coaches teach the wrist rolls through at contact. This drill trains the stay-through version. Then: bottom hand only. 10 swings. Feel the difference: bottom hand drives the barrel, top hand guides it. Then: both hands. 10 swings. Feel the integration of both.
cue: One widely-taught approach: keep the top hand palm up at contact to prevent rolling over early. Bottom hand drives the barrel through.
why: One-hand drills are common in hitting practice. They let a hitter feel what each hand does before putting the swing back together.
watch: Wrist rolling over before contact. In this approach, palm should face up or outward at the moment of contact. Bottom-hand swings collapsing at contact.
harder: Top-hand-only soft toss instead of tee. Progress to full swing with emphasis on hand roles.
easier: Slow-motion swings first. Have the hitter stop at contact and check hand position before completing.

title: Hit to the Gap
gear: Coach pitch or tee, cones marking gaps, field
setup: Mark the left-center and right-center gaps with cones. Coach pitches or hitter hits off tee.
how: Mark two gap zones with cones: left-center and right-center. Coach pitches or hitter hits off tee. Ball must land between the gap cones to score a point. Pull-side or foul = no point. Opposite field line = no point (too far). 20 swings. Track gap percentage. Debrief: what adjustments did you make to reach the gap?
cue: Drive it up the middle. Let the gap find you.
why: Aiming for the gaps encourages hard line drives up the middle instead of trying to pull everything. The cones give a clear target.
watch: Hitter pulling everything. Reinforce "stay through the middle." Swinging up to create loft. Contact should be line-drive height.
harder: Alternate gap. Two swings to left-center gap, two to right-center. Add a fielder in the gap who scores a point for catches.
easier: No cones. Just ask the hitter to aim for up the middle on every swing.

title: Glove-to-Hand Exchange Drill
setup: Player stands alone. Ball in glove.
how: Player stands with a ball in their glove. On "go": transfer the ball from glove to throwing grip as fast as possible. Time it with a phone stopwatch or count "one thousand one" in your head. Goal: beat your own best time. 25 reps. Progress: start from a simulated fielding position. Ball rolling into your glove from a roll, then transfer. The roll adds the real-game feel.
cue: Two hands. Glove meets throwing hand, not the other way.
why: A quick, clean transfer saves time on every throw. It is easy to practice alone and easy to time, so kids can see themselves improve.
watch: Reaching into the glove with the throwing hand instead of meeting it at the waist. Grip not being a proper four-seam on the transfer.
harder: Add the transfer and a throw to a target. Time from catch to ball leaving the hand.
easier: Slow motion. Count: "catch, transfer, grip." Check each step before speeding up.

title: Behind-the-Back Catch
setup: Partners 8-10 feet apart. One player puts their glove (or catching hand) behind their back.
how: Partners 8-10 feet apart. Catcher puts dominant hand (or glove) behind their back. Partner makes soft underhand tosses. Varying left, right, and directly to the catcher. Catcher must sense where the ball is and catch it behind their back with one hand. 15 tosses each. Progress: toss from 12 feet. Add a light bounce off the ground before catching.
cue: Feel where the ball is. Trust your hands.
why: A fun coordination challenge. Kids learn to feel where the ball is and trust their hands.
watch: Catcher peeking around their body. They must keep looking forward. Partner tossing too hard. Keep it soft.
harder: Tosser uses overhand instead of underhand. Add a secondary task: catcher counts backward from 10 simultaneously.
easier: Tosser bounces the ball softly. Slower trajectory gives more time to locate.

title: Accuracy Tournament
gear: Balls, gloves, target on fence or strike zone
setup: Tape a 2x2 foot square target on a fence or backstop at chest height. Players stand at three distances: 30, 45, 60 feet.
how: Tape a 2x2 foot target on a fence or backstop at chest height. Divide the target into 4 quadrants with tape. Players start at 30 feet: 5 throws, mark which quadrant each hits. Move to 45 feet: 5 more. Then 60 feet: 5 more. Scoring: bull's-eye center = 3 pts, quadrant hit = 2 pts, target edge = 1 pt, miss = 0. Track scores, run bracket: high scores advance.
cue: Pick a spot inside the target. Not the whole square.
why: A tournament turns accuracy practice into something kids care about. Competition usually brings more effort than solo throwing.
watch: Players gunning for velocity instead of accuracy. This is a precision drill. No pre-throw target selection.
harder: Add a time limit per throw. Require the thrower to call which quadrant before throwing.
easier: Larger target (4x4 feet). Two distances only: 20 and 35 feet.

title: Cross-Body Throwing Drill
setup: Player starts facing away from their throwing target. Partner gives a "go" signal.
how: Player starts facing completely away from their throwing target. Partner calls "go." Player pivots on their throwing-side foot. Spin to face the target. Find the target with eyes. Then plant the glove-side foot and throw. 15 reps facing full opposite. Then 10 reps facing 90 degrees right. Then 10 reps facing 90 degrees left. Simulate a shortstop making a spin throw.
cue: Find your target with your feet first. Then throw.
why: Fielders often have to turn and throw instead of throwing from a set position. This gives reps finding the target with the feet first.
watch: Throwing before eyes find the target. Throwing off the back foot. Must plant glove-side foot first.
harder: Add a baserunner who starts running on "go." Fielder must complete the spin and throw in time.
easier: Walk through in slow motion: pivot, find target, plant, throw. No speed yet.

title: Receive and Redirect
gear: Balls, gloves, three players in triangle
setup: Three players in a triangle 25-30 feet apart. Ball starts at player 1.
how: Three players in a triangle 25-30 feet apart. Player 1 throws to Player 2. Player 2 catches and immediately, while still moving to the ball, redirects a throw to Player 3. Player 3 catches moving and throws to Player 1. The rule: you cannot set your feet before throwing. Catch and redirect in one motion. 20 complete cycles. Debrief: what makes a good on-the-move throw?
cue: Catch it moving. Throw it moving. Stay athletic.
why: Many game throws happen on the move: relays, double plays, cutoffs. This gives practice catching and throwing without setting up first.
watch: Players stopping to set feet before throwing. Enforce the rule. Throws going to the wrong player.
harder: Increase the triangle distances. Add a fourth player. Put a time limit on the redirect.
easier: Allow one additional step to plant before throwing. Start at 15-foot distances.

title: Relay Race with Scoring
gear: Balls, gloves, buckets or bases at relay stations
setup: 3 relay stations at 40-foot intervals. Two teams compete on parallel tracks.
how: Two parallel relay tracks with stations 40 feet apart. Ball starts at station 1. Throw to station 2, who throws to station 3, who throws back. Each dropped ball must be picked up before continuing. No skipping. Each overthrow past the next player: that player jogs to retrieve it. Team with most completed relays in 90 seconds wins. Play 3 rounds.
cue: Throw to the chest. Make it easy on your teammate.
why: Relay races are a classic. The race adds urgency, and chest-high throws win, so kids learn that accuracy beats arm strength.
watch: Players throwing too hard causing overthrows. Chest-high throws win. Station players not getting in ready position between throws.
harder: Add a fourth station. Require a crow hop before each throw.
easier: Allow one bounce between stations. Reduce to two stations only.

title: Jump Read Drill
gear: Full field, ball, pitcher on mound
setup: Runner at first. Coach in pitcher position with ball, working from the stretch. No hitter. Use only where leads and pickoffs are allowed (not Little League 12U and younger, not fastpitch softball).
how: Runner takes a primary lead at first. Coach or pitcher comes set and delivers from the stretch. Runner must read the front hip of the pitcher: front hip commits to home = take secondary lead. Front hip turns toward first = get back. Run 15 reads. Coach randomly mixes pickoffs and pitches. No one tells the runner which is coming. After 5 reps, ask: "What are you watching?"
cue: Pick one spot on the pitcher, like the front hip or heel, and read it.
why: Runners get a better jump when they watch one part of the pitcher instead of the ball. The front hip or heel is a common cue; coaches differ, so pick one and stick with it.
watch: Runner watching the hands or the ball instead of the front hip. Late reads.
harder: Add a real first baseman receiving pickoff throws. Live pitch situation with a real catcher.
easier: Coach verbally labels the move as "pickoff" or "pitch" at first. Runners just practice the footwork response.

title: Delayed Steal Timing
setup: Runner at second or first. Live catcher receiving pitches. No hitter.
how: Runner at first or second. Coach pitches to a live catcher. After the catcher catches and begins throwing back to the pitcher: runner goes. The exact cue: the moment the ball leaves the catcher's throwing hand. Run 8 attempts from each base. Debrief after all attempts: what timing cue worked best?
cue: Go when the ball leaves the catcher. Not after.
why: The delayed steal catches a defense relaxing on the throw back to the pitcher. It takes exact timing, so it needs practice.
watch: Runner going too early. Must wait for the catcher to commit to the return throw. Runner going too late. The pitcher is already receiving and looking.
harder: Real fielders who attempt to make the play. Mix in situations where the delay steal is not on.
easier: Coach stands behind the catcher and verbally cues "now" at the right moment for the first 5 attempts.

title: Lead-Off Technique at First
setup: Runner at first. Pitcher on mound. First baseman at bag. Use only where leads are allowed (not Little League 12U and younger, not fastpitch softball).
how: Runner takes their primary lead: 3-4 shuffle steps off first, weight on balls of feet, knees bent. Pitcher delivers from the stretch: runner takes 2 secondary shuffle steps. Pitcher picks off: runner gets back to the bag. Run 10 pitch reads and 5 pickoff reads. Measure lead distance with a cone placed at the runner's feet. Track whether lead is consistent or shrinking due to fear of pickoff.
cue: Stay low in your lead. You're not standing, you're ready to run.
why: Lead distance and posture are habits. A low, ready lead helps a runner react faster in either direction.
watch: Runner standing straight up in their lead. Lead shrinking because they're afraid. Keep the lead distance consistent.
harder: Add a real first baseman who catches pickoffs. Runner tries to steal on a read.
easier: Practice the footwork only. No pitcher. Just take the lead and return 20 times.

title: Tag-Up Reads
setup: Runner on third. Outfielder positioned in different spots. Coach hits flies at various depths.
how: Runner at third. Outfielder in various spots. Coach hits fly balls at different depths: very shallow, medium, and deep. Runner keeps one foot on third until the ball hits the glove. Moment of contact: runner goes. For shallow flies: runner should stay. For deep flies: runner goes. After 10 reps, ask runner: "What made you decide to go or stay?" They must have a reason.
cue: Leave the moment the ball touches the glove, not after.
why: Tagging up is easy to get wrong in the moment. Reps teach runners to be on the bag and ready to leave the moment the ball is touched.
watch: Runner leaving before the catch. Runner going on shallow flies when they should hold.
harder: Add a real throw home. Runner reads the throw and decides to score or hold.
easier: Coach calls "go" or "hold" for the first 5 reps. Runner focuses on the tagging footwork before adding the read.

title: Hustle-to-First Competition
setup: Players line up at home plate in batting stance. Coach at the mound.
how: Players line up at home plate in batting stance. Coach signals. Player breaks and sprints through first base. Must run through, never stopping. Touch the front edge of the bag. After crossing, break down and look right for an overthrow. In softball, use the orange safety base if your league has one. Time each player and post their time. Compete to improve personal bests each week.
cue: Run through the base. Don't stop AT it.
why: Running through first is one of the most common baserunning fixes for young players, and reps fix it. Timing adds urgency.
watch: Slowing down before the bag. Stopping on the bag. Not looking right.
harder: Add a live batted ball. Time the player from the swing.
easier: Walk through the motion first before sprinting.

title: Two-Out Running Reads
setup: Runner on base. Two outs declared. Live fielders. Coach hits or rolls.
how: Announce "two outs" before each rep. Coach hits or rolls to various positions. Runner goes on contact regardless. No coaching during the rep. Just run. After each rep, pause and ask the runner: "What's the rule with two outs?" Let them say it. Mix in a pop-up and a line drive: with two outs, the runner still goes.
cue: Two outs, you run on contact. Period.
why: Two-out running is a simple rule kids forget in the moment. Practicing it makes it automatic, and it can turn close plays into runs.
watch: Runner hesitating on any batted ball. With two outs there is nothing to read: run.
harder: Live fielders who make real plays. Full inning with score.
easier: Coach rolls only. No surprises. Slowly add variety after the rule is understood.

title: Base-Rounding Angle Race
gear: Full base set, cones marking wide arc
setup: Cones mark a rounding arc a few feet outside the baseline, starting about 15 feet before each base. Players compete in pairs from home.
how: Place cones a few feet outside the baseline, about 15 feet before first and second base, to mark the arc. Two players race from home. Both must loop around the outside of the arc cone before touching each base. Player who ignores the cone and runs straight loses the point regardless of speed. Five races per round. Best of 5 wins the series.
cue: Loop wide early. Hit the inside corner of the bag.
why: A good turn lets runners keep their speed through the base instead of stopping to change direction. The cones make the arc visible, and racing makes kids want to do it right.
watch: Players cutting inside the cone. Players forgetting the cone once they get competitive.
harder: Add a third base cone. Time each player individually and compare.
easier: Walk the cone path first. Show how the arc lets you keep running hard through the base.

title: Dirt Ball Reads
gear: Full battery, runner at base, ball
setup: Runner at first, second, or third. Pitcher throws to catcher. Catcher intentionally or unintentionally blocks some balls in the dirt.
how: Runner on first, second, or third. Coach throws to a live catcher. Mix: (1) clean catches, (2) intentional balls in the dirt the catcher blocks, (3) passed balls. Runner reads each pitch. Clean catch: hold. Blocked and kept in front: hold. Blocked and kicked away, or a passed ball: go. No verbal cues. Runner reads only. After 10 pitches, ask: "What were you watching?"
cue: Watch the ball into the mitt. Not the catcher's body.
why: Balls in the dirt happen a lot in youth games. Runners who read them well can take extra bases, and this gives many reads in a short time.
watch: Runner watching the catcher's body instead of the ball. Not going on a passed ball. Going on a blocked ball that was controlled.
harder: Add a runner at third who scores on a passed ball. Mix in pickoff attempts.
easier: Coach calls each pitch type before throwing. Runner just practices the response.

title: Five-Pitch Game
setup: Two teams. Coach pitches. Batter gets exactly 5 pitches per at-bat regardless of count.
how: Two teams. Coach pitches. Five pitches per batter regardless of count. After five pitches: if no contact, it's an out. Result: best contact among five pitches. Hitter must swing at strikes. Taking a perfect strike is an automatic out. After each half-inning, ask one fielder: "What was the most important play that inning?"
cue: Know which pitch you want before it comes.
why: Keeps the pace up and makes hitters decisive. No walks means more balls in play and more action for the fielders.
watch: Batters taking obvious strikes. Enforce the rule. Fielders relaxing because contact is guaranteed.
harder: Reduce to three pitches. Add a 'best contact' scoring: line drive = double, grounder through = single.
easier: No time limit. Batter keeps getting pitches until contact is made.

title: Field Home Run Derby
gear: Wiffle balls, plastic bat, cones marking HR line
setup: Two teams. Cone line 60 feet from home = home run. Players rotate through batting.
how: Cone line 60 feet from home = home run. Players rotate: each gets 5 swings off a tee or coach pitch. Ball over the line = 1 point. Ball through the infield = half a point. Between turns: fielders retrieve and reset balls. Teams tally points after each full rotation. Run 3 rotations. Final rotation: announce before each swing which field the hitter is targeting. Bonus point for hitting the announced field.
cue: Drive it. Get on top and through the ball.
why: A home run line gives kids a fun, clear goal. Team scoring makes every swing matter to them.
watch: Players swinging only for power. Encourage driving through the ball rather than trying to uppercut.
harder: Move the cone back. Add a fielder in the outfield who catches home runs for the opposing team.
easier: No competition. Just count home runs individually and celebrate each one.

title: Pickle (Rundown)
gear: Two bases 45 feet apart, balls, gloves
setup: Two fielders, one on each base with a ball. One runner starts in between.
how: Two fielders, one at each base with a ball. Runner starts in the middle. Fielder with ball runs at the runner to shorten the throw. Runner tries to avoid tags by changing direction. Key: fielder should have to throw at most once to get the runner out. Change the runner every 3 rundowns. Score: fielders get a point for each out made in one throw or less.
cue: Run hard at the runner. Make the throw as short as possible.
why: Rundowns come up in games but rarely get practiced. A few reps give fielders a plan: run at the runner and keep throws short.
watch: Fielders making 3-4 throws. Reinforce running at the runner. Fielder throwing to the wrong base.
harder: Add a third fielder. Add a time limit: if the runner survives 15 seconds, they're safe.
easier: Walk speed only. Fielders toss instead of throw. Practice the pattern without any defense first.

title: Ghost Runner Game
setup: Two players: one bats, one fields (rotates to pitch next). Ghost runners on base (imaginary). Normal batting order.
how: Two players minimum. One bats, one pitches (or coach pitches). Ghost runners occupy bases based on contact results: single advances all ghosts one base, double two bases, etc. Batter tracks ghost runner positions out loud after each hit. After 5 outs, switch. Batter who scores the most ghost runs wins. Batter must narrate: "Ghost runner on second would score on that double. That's one run."
cue: Advance the ghost runner. That's your job.
why: Lets small groups play real baseball with situations. Great for low-attendance days.
watch: Players losing track of ghost runner positions. Not advancing ghost runners on contact.
harder: Two batters alternating. One plays for each team. Add real baserunning for the batter themselves.
easier: Just one ghost runner at a fixed base. Track if they score or not.

title: Defense-Only Competitive Game
gear: Full field, coach or machine feeding
setup: Split team into two defensive units. Coach hits or rolls balls. One unit fields, one watches and evaluates.
how: Split team into two defensive units of 4-5 players. Coach feeds balls (grounders, pop-ups, line drives) one at a time. First unit fields. Points: correct fielding + throw to right base = 1 point. Error or wrong decision = 0. Watching unit evaluates: one player per play says what the fielding team did right or wrong. After 8 plays, switch. Track points.
cue: Right play fast. Wrong play, no points.
why: Puts the focus on defense and good decisions. Points for the right play, not just outs, reward thinking.
watch: Evaluating players being harsh. Remind them they are looking for one thing done right AND one thing to improve.
harder: Add a runner to create real time pressure. Watching team can buzz in with a challenge if they think the call was wrong.
easier: No score. Just field and give constructive verbal feedback.

title: Hit and Run Live
setup: Runner on first. Hitter at plate. Full infield. Coach pitches.
how: Runner on first. Full infield. Before every pitch: offense secretly decides hit-and-run or no. If hit-and-run: runner goes on the pitch, batter must put it in play. Successful hit-and-run (batter makes contact + runner advances) = 2 points. Failed (batter misses, runner caught) = defense gets 1 point. Play 3 innings of 3 outs each.
cue: Hitter: put it on the ground right side. Runner: trust it and go.
why: The hit-and-run needs the runner and hitter to trust each other. Playing it live builds that timing.
watch: Runner not going when called. Batter swinging late on the hit-and-run. They must swing at anything.
harder: Runner can also attempt a straight steal. Adds decision complexity for the defense.
easier: Walk through the communication first: batter nods to runner, runner acknowledges. Run 5 practice reps before scoring.

title: One-Pitch Game
gear: Soft balls, bases at 40 ft, gloves
setup: Coach pitches. Each batter gets ONE strike to work with. Take a ball and you get another pitch.
how: Coach pitches. One pitch per batter. Batter chooses: swing or take. Swing and miss = out. Take a strike = out. Take a ball = one more pitch. Ball put in play = live. Fast rotation. Next batter up immediately after each play. Fielders must pre-set before every pitch. Three outs per inning, 4 innings. Coach narrates after each play: "One pitch. What did you decide?"
cue: One pitch. Make it count.
why: Creates urgency, keeps energy high, and packs a lot of at-bats into a short time.
watch: Batters taking pitches out of fear. Fielders not pre-setting.
harder: Player pitching. More realistic pitch location variation. Add a stolen base option for the runner.
easier: No outs. Everyone hits and runs for 2 full rotations before adding the out rule.

title: Continuous Baserunning Game
setup: All players are runners distributed around the bases. One fielder in the middle with a ball.
how: Players distribute across all four bases. One fielder in the center with a ball. On "go": all runners attempt to advance simultaneously to the next base. Fielder can tag any runner caught between bases. Tagged runner becomes the new fielder. Old fielder joins the base rotation. Keep score: how long can you stay untagged? Player tagged fewest times over 10 rounds wins.
cue: Run hard. Being between bases is dangerous.
why: Lots of running with a built-in reason to run hard. The tag game makes hustle feel like part of the fun.
watch: Runners walking instead of running. Fielder standing in the middle instead of chasing.
harder: Two fielders in the middle. Fielders can throw to bases instead of only tagging.
easier: One fielder, slow rolling to each base to demonstrate the concept before going full speed.

title: Windup vs. Stretch Strike Count
setup: Pitcher alternates: one pitch from windup, one from stretch. Catcher or net at league distance.
how: Pitcher alternates: one pitch from the windup, one from the stretch. After each pair, the pitcher answers one question out loud: "Which one felt more comfortable?" 10 pairs of pitches. Track windup strikes vs. stretch strikes on a simple tally. Count every pitch toward the day's pitch count.
cue: Same target, same routine, from both starts.
why: Pitchers throw from the stretch whenever runners are on, so they need reps there too. A simple strike tally shows where they are more comfortable. Keep feedback on the target, not the delivery.
watch: Pitcher rushing the pace from the stretch. Frustration after misses: count strikes, not misses. Any arm pain: stop for the day.
harder: A full session from the stretch, since runners on base put pitchers there often.
easier: Walk through the windup and stretch with no ball first to learn the legal starting positions.

title: Pitcher Fielding Practice (PFP)
setup: Pitcher on mound. Fielders at first and third. Coach at home.
how: Pitcher simulates a delivery without a ball (to save pitches). Coach at home plate immediately rolls or bunts a ball. Pitcher fields it and throws to the correct base. Mix in: (1) ball to the first base side: pitcher covers first, (2) bunt down the third base line: pitcher fields and throws to first, (3) comebacker: throw to first or second depending on the runner. 12 situations.
cue: Ball hit back to you? You are an infielder now.
why: The pitcher is the fifth infielder but rarely gets fielding reps. Comebackers, bunts, and covering first come up in games and can be practiced.
watch: Pitcher not breaking to first on balls hit to the right side. Throws to the wrong base.
harder: Add a live runner creating real time pressure. Mix in line drives back through the box.
easier: Coach rolls slow comebackers while the pitcher starts in a ready position on the mound. Walk through covering first.

title: Charted Bullpen Session
gear: Ball, catcher, paper strike zone chart
setup: Draw a simple strike zone divided into 9 zones (3x3 grid) on paper. Catcher calls targets by zone number.
how: Draw a 3x3 strike zone grid on paper. 9 zones numbered. Catcher calls a zone number before each pitch. Pitcher throws to that zone. Mark hit vs. miss on the chart after each pitch. 20 pitches. After: find the 3 zones with the worst accuracy. Add 5 extra pitches to each weak zone. Pitcher keeps the chart for next session and tracks it over time. Count every pitch toward the daily limit.
cue: Know your chart. Attack your strong zones in games.
why: Charting shows a pitcher where their misses tend to go, which makes practice more specific. Keep it about targets, not delivery changes, and count every pitch.
watch: Pitcher guessing zone location instead of having a real target. Catcher not setting up in the called zone.
harder: Add a batter who is allowed to take. Pitcher must throw actual strikes.
easier: Only 4 zones: up/down/in/out. 10 pitches. Simple chart.

title: Pitcher Covers First
setup: Pitcher on the mound. First baseman at first. Coach at home with balls.
how: Pitcher starts on the mound in a ready position (no pitch thrown). Coach rolls a grounder to the first baseman. Pitcher breaks toward a spot a few feet up the first base line, then runs along the line to the bag. First baseman fields and gives a chest-high underhand toss. Pitcher catches, touches the inside edge of the bag, and turns toward the infield to stay out of the runner's path. 10 reps. Then mix in balls the first baseman takes to the bag alone: pitcher peels off.
cue: Ball to the right side, you break for first.
why: Covering first is a fielding job pitchers need to learn. It is footwork and communication, no delivery work, and it saves outs.
watch: Pitcher running straight at the bag and into the runner's path. Pitcher watching the grounder instead of breaking to first.
harder: Add a runner. Mix in balls the first baseman fields near the bag so the pitcher has to read whether to keep going.
easier: Walk through the route with no ball: break, run up the line, touch the bag, turn inside.

title: Process Goal Setting
setup: Start of practice or season. Each player writes or says one process goal.
how: Each player takes a card or phone. Completes this sentence: "Today I will focus on ______." Goal must pass the behavior test: it describes something the player does, not something that happens. Coach reviews each goal before practice starts: valid = behavior ("I will call for every pop-up"), invalid = outcome ("I will make no errors"). At the end of practice: each player rates how well they stuck to their goal. 1 to 5.
cue: What you do. Not what happens.
why: Process goals keep attention on what the player controls. Sport psychology research generally supports them, mostly with older athletes. One small goal per practice is easy to do.
watch: Players writing outcome goals. Players writing goals that are impossible to observe.
harder: Players write a weekly goal in addition to a daily one. Players pair up and check each other's goals.
easier: Coach provides three goal options and players choose one.

title: Pre-Pitch Routine Training
setup: In the batter's box or on the mound. No ball yet.
how: Coach explains: the routine is 3 steps, always the same. For hitters: (1) step out of the box, (2) tap the bat twice, (3) look to the third base coach, step in. For pitchers: (1) step on the rubber, (2) look at the target for 2 seconds, (3) set and deliver. Practice the routine 10 times without a ball. Then incorporate it into a live at-bat or pitch sequence. Enforce it every single rep.
cue: Same routine every time.
why: Routines give players something familiar to do when they feel nervous. Being consistent matters more than what the routine is. They are widely used in sport; research support is mostly with older athletes.
watch: Players skipping steps when they are in a hurry. Routines taking too long and slowing the game.
harder: Add a mental component between steps 2 and 3: one breath. Progress to enforcing the routine in competition.
easier: Two-step routine only. Build to three steps.

title: Sock Ball Soft Toss
setup: Stuff an old sock with rags or tape it into a ball shape. Hold the bat in your bottom hand and the sock ball in your top hand at waist height.
how: Stand in batting stance. Bat in your bottom hand, sock ball or wiffle ball in your top hand at waist height. Flip it upward with a gentle underhand motion. 12-18 inches above the contact zone. Get both hands on the bat and let it fall to your contact point. Swing through it. Focus: hands back until the ball reaches the contact zone. Not when it's at the top of the flip.
cue: Drive through it. Don't just hit it.
why: A sock ball is a free way to get self-toss swings anywhere. The soft contact gives a feel for driving through the ball versus slapping at it.
watch: Swinging while the ball is still rising.
harder: Flip to different heights randomly.
easier: Flip only 6 inches. Almost no arc. Very slow decision.

title: High-Low Tee Work
setup: Set tee at high (letter height), take 5 swings. Set tee at low (knee height), take 5 swings. Alternate without resetting your stance.
how: Tee at letter-height: 10 swings. Tee at knee-height: 10 swings. Now alternate randomly. Call the height before each swing, then move the tee. 20 total. Check: for high ball, keep path level. For low ball, slight downward angle to the contact point. The body should adjust naturally if you trust the contact point.
cue: High: flat path. Low: slight downward angle. Both: drive through.
why: Pitches come at different heights, so tee work at one height only covers part of the zone. Alternating makes you adjust.
watch: Same swing path regardless of height.
harder: Add inside/outside to the high/low variation. Four variables total.
easier: One height per session.

title: One-Hand Catch and Toss
setup: Stand 8 feet from wall. Throwing hand holds the ball.
how: Throwing hand holds a tennis ball. Throw it at the wall with your throwing hand. Catch the rebound with your non-dominant (glove-side) hand only. 20 reps. The catch must be one-handed. Teaches the non-dominant hand to be active. Then switch: throw with non-dominant hand, catch with dominant.
cue: Soft catch. Give with the ball.
why: Builds coordination in the glove-side hand. A simple solo hands drill that works anywhere there is a wall.
watch: Using both hands to catch. Non-dominant hand only.
harder: Increase the throw intensity.
easier: Bounce the ball off the floor. Slower rebound.

title: Situational Tee Work
setup: Mark three zones with cones beyond the net: left field, center, right. Announce a situation before each swing.
how: Before each swing: announce a situation. Set the tee accordingly. Swing with that purpose. "Runner on second, no outs: hit to the right side." Set tee on outside corner. Drive it the other way. "Need a fly ball: runner on third, one out." Adjust swing angle upward. 15 situational swings. Grade yourself: did the ball go where the situation required?
cue: Know the situation. Hit with purpose.
why: Adds a purpose to each tee swing. Hitting to a situation is closer to a game than swinging just to make contact.
watch: Setting up the situation then swinging the same way as always.
harder: Record yourself and review: did the ball actually go where you intended?
easier: Just two situations alternating: hit to right side vs. hit for power.

title: Phone Video Swing Analysis
setup: Prop phone in video mode at knee height, facing home plate from the front. Get the whole swing in frame.
how: Prop phone on video mode at knee height facing home plate. Take 10 swings. After each: watch the video immediately. Focus on ONE thing per session. Pick before you start. Example: "I'm checking if my back heel comes up before contact." After 10 swings: make one adjustment. Take 10 more. Compare.
cue: Watch. Then change one thing. One thing.
why: Video is a free self-coaching tool if you have a phone. The one-thing rule keeps you from trying to fix everything at once.
watch: Checking multiple things. Pick one.
harder: Slow the video to 0.25x speed. Compare side-by-side with a pro swing you've saved.
easier: Watch 5 swings before making any adjustment.

title: Staircase Grounders
setup: Stand 10 feet from the base of a staircase. Roll or throw the tennis ball at the bottom step.
how: Stand 10 feet from the base of a staircase. Roll or throw a tennis ball at the bottom step. It bounces off at an unpredictable angle. Field 20 bounces. No glove for first 10 reps. Add glove for the second 10. Vary which step you hit to change the rebound speed and angle.
cue: Stay wide and low. The bounce will pick a side.
why: The steps create odd bounces, like bad hops on a real field. Good for quick hands and staying low.
watch: Trying to predict the bounce. Standing too far. Move closer for faster returns.
harder: Hit higher steps for wilder angles.
easier: Throw very softly so the rebound is slow and more predictable.

title: Two-Ball Juggling
setup: Stand still. Hold one tennis ball in each hand.
how: Hold one tennis ball in each hand. Toss the right-hand ball straight up. As it peaks, toss the left-hand ball up. Catch the first ball in the left hand as the second ball peaks. Catch the second in the right hand. Repeat. Count consecutive catches. Goal: 10+ in a row. Rest 30 seconds. Three sets.
cue: Toss. Then catch. Don't grab at it.
why: Juggling is a fun hand-eye and timing challenge that builds patience and hand independence. Whether it improves fielding directly is not well studied.
watch: Throwing sideways instead of straight up.
harder: Three-ball juggling.
easier: Toss one ball up and catch it first. Then add the second.

title: Glove Transfer Reps
setup: Sit or stand. Ball in glove.
how: Ball in glove. Transfer to throwing grip as fast as possible. Time it and try to beat your best. 25 reps. Progress: start from a fielding position (simulate a grounder coming into your glove from a roll) then transfer. The simulated field adds the real-game feel. Check: are you setting a four-seam grip on every transfer?
cue: Two thumbs together on the transfer. Glove meets hand at the waist.
why: A fast, clean transfer saves time on every throw, and it only takes a ball and a glove to practice.
watch: Not setting a proper grip. Rotating the ball to four-seam before throwing.
harder: Add a throw to a wall target immediately after transfer.
easier: Slow motion. Count: "catch, transfer, grip." Check each step.

title: Angle Throws to Wall
setup: Stand 12 feet from a wall at a 45-degree angle to it (not facing it straight-on).
how: Stand 12 feet from a wall at a 45-degree angle. Throw the ball into the wall. It bounces back at the opposite angle. Requiring lateral movement to field it. Move your feet to the ball. Never reach. 20 reps. Then reverse sides: stand at 45 degrees in the other direction.
cue: Move your feet first. Don't reach.
why: Angled rebounds make you move sideways to the ball instead of fielding it straight on, which is closer to many game grounders.
watch: Reaching for the rebound instead of moving feet.
harder: Move to 8 feet for faster returns.
easier: Straight-on throws only until comfortable, then add the angle.

title: Self-Toss Fly Ball Tracking
setup: Open field. Player tosses the ball straight up as high as possible.
how: Stand in open field. Toss the ball straight up as high as you can. 40-50 feet. Track it and catch in the glove. 15 catches. Progress: jog 5-10 steps in a direction, then toss the ball over your opposite shoulder and run to it. This replicates the over-the-shoulder fly ball read.
cue: Find it early. Move your feet before you look for the ball.
why: The easiest outfield drill there is. The high toss gives tracking practice, and the over-the-shoulder version works on a tough play.
watch: Watching the toss instead of immediately tracking the arc.
harder: Sprint instead of jog before the toss.
easier: Toss only 20 feet high. Shorter tracking window.

title: Four-Seam Grip by Feel
setup: Sit or stand. One baseball.
how: Hold one baseball. Set a four-seam grip (fingers across the wide seams). Release and re-grip 10 times without looking. Toss the ball 6 inches up, catch it, and set the four-seam grip as fast as you can. 20 times. Goal: four-seam grip without looking, every time.
cue: Find the seams without looking.
why: A four-seam grip helps throws fly straight. Finding it by feel speeds up the transfer. It takes only a ball and a few minutes.
watch: Looking at the ball to set the grip.
harder: Set grip and throw to a target in one fluid motion.
easier: Look at the ball for grip setting. Gradually reduce how long you look.

title: Wall Crow Hop Throws
setup: Stand 25-30 feet from wall. Get into fielding position.
how: Stand 25-30 feet from a wall in fielding position. Simulate fielding a grounder (touch the ground with glove). Crow hop (hop onto the throwing-side foot, then step toward the target with the glove-side foot). Throw at a wall target. Field the rebound. Repeat. Every throw includes the full crow hop. No exceptions. 20 reps.
cue: Crow hop before every long throw. Always.
why: The crow hop gives young outfielders a simple footwork pattern to get moving toward the target on longer throws. The wall makes it a solo drill. Keep throws at comfortable effort.
watch: Skipping the crow hop and throwing flat-footed.
harder: Increase to 35 feet.
easier: Walk through the crow hop footwork 10 times without a ball first.

title: Turn and Throw to the Fence
setup: Mark a chest-high target on a fence or backstop. Stand 30-45 feet away, facing away from the fence.
how: Stand 30-45 feet from a fence target, facing away from it. Toss the ball up to yourself and catch it. Turn toward your glove side, find the target with your eyes, and throw. Hit = 1 point. Collect balls every 5 throws. 15-20 throws at comfortable effort, never max. Stop if your arm is sore.
cue: Catch, turn glove side, find it, throw.
why: Practices the catch, turn, and throw a relay player makes, with a target for feedback. Keep the throw count modest and the effort comfortable.
watch: Turning the wrong way (toward the throwing-hand side). Throwing before the eyes find the target. Max-effort throws.
harder: Shorten the time between catch and throw. Add a partner who calls a new target each rep.
easier: Face the target and just catch and throw at 20-30 feet.

title: Shadow Routine Rehearsal
setup: On a mound or flat ground. No ball.
how: No ball. Rehearse your routine 10 times: step on the rubber, look in for the sign, pick a target, take one breath, then an easy dry motion at half speed. Then 5 more at game pace. The goal is doing the routine the same way every time.
cue: Same routine, every pitch.
why: Rehearsing the routine without a ball gives reps with no arm stress and helps the routine feel automatic. We leave delivery changes to a qualified pitching coach.
watch: Skipping steps. Rushing the breath.
harder: Rehearse with a teammate calling game situations: "Runner on first, 2-1 count."
easier: 5 rehearsals. Just the step, the target, and the breath.

title: Four-Zone Wall Targets
setup: Put four tape targets on a wall in a 2x2 pattern: top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right. Start 20 feet away.
how: Put four tape targets on a wall in a 2x2 pattern: top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right. Start 20 feet away. Call the zone before each throw. 3 throws per zone, 12 total. Score yourself. Move to 30 feet and repeat. Compare accuracy by zone. Find your worst zone and throw 5 extra to it.
cue: Call it, see it, throw to it.
why: Four targets give you a score and show which zone you miss most. Knowing that tells you where to practice.
watch: Not calling the zone before throwing.
harder: Move to 40 feet.
easier: Two zones only: high and low. Larger targets.

title: Box Jumps or Step Jumps
setup: Stable surface 8-12 inches high. Stand facing it.
how: Stand facing a step or box 8-12 inches high. Two-foot jump onto the surface. Drive with the arms. Land softly: both feet, knees bent, absorb the landing. Step back down (do not jump down). 3 sets of 8 jumps. Rest 45 seconds between sets. Add: pause at the top for 2 seconds. Hold the landing before stepping down.
cue: Land like you're trying not to make noise.
why: Builds leg power and teaches soft, controlled landings. Stepping down instead of jumping down keeps the impact low.
watch: Landing with straight knees: absorb the impact. During growth spurts, cut the sets in half and stop if knees or heels are sore.
harder: Hold the landing 3 seconds. Single-leg landings for older, experienced players only.
easier: Step onto the box with one foot first instead of jumping.

title: Light Medicine Ball Rotational Throws
gear: Light medicine ball (2-4 lb) or basketball, wall
setup: Stand sideways to wall, 3-4 feet away. Hold medicine ball at chest.
how: Stand sideways to a wall 3-4 feet away. Hold a light ball (2-4 lb) at chest. Rotate away from the wall. Loading. Drive hips back toward the wall, then let the shoulders follow. Release the ball into the wall. Catch the rebound. 10 reps each side. Hips start the throw. Arms just deliver it. Rest 45 seconds between sides.
cue: Hips start the throw. Arms just deliver it.
why: Practices turning the hips and trunk together with a light ball. Keep it light: this is about rhythm and control, not heavy loading.
watch: Arms doing all the work. Not rotating fully before throwing. Using a heavy ball: stay light.
harder: Step into the throw. Add a few reps with the same light ball.
easier: No ball. Just practice the rotation pattern 20 times.

title: T-Balance Hold
setup: Stand on one foot. Arms out to the sides.
how: Stand on one foot. Lean forward until your body forms a T. Torso parallel to ground, free leg extending behind. Arms out to the sides for balance. Hold 10 seconds. 5 holds per leg. Close your eyes for the last 2 holds.
cue: Find one point on the floor. Hold still.
why: Builds single-leg balance and hip control, which help with fielding, running, and just about every athletic move.
watch: Hips rotating open. Keep hips square to the ground.
harder: Hold while catching a tennis ball tossed to you.
easier: Hold for 5 seconds only. Touch a wall if needed.

title: Advanced Ladder Patterns
setup: Agility ladder on flat ground. Advanced patterns require 10+ ladder rungs.
how: Advanced ladder patterns on flat ground. Pattern 1: single-leg hops through each box. Pattern 2: lateral icky shuffle. In-in-out-out sideways. Pattern 3: hip rotation. Step in each box and turn 90 degrees. 3 runs through each pattern. 30-second rest. Arms pump hard. They drive the rhythm.
cue: Arms drive the rhythm. Pump them hard.
why: Harder patterns challenge coordination and keep ladder work interesting for older players.
watch: Looking down at the ladder. During growth spurts, drop the single-leg hops.
harder: Add a sprint for 10 yards after exiting the ladder.
easier: Basic one-foot-in-each-box at walk speed.

title: Sprint Mechanics Drill
setup: 30-yard lane. Phone on video if self-coaching.
how: 30-yard lane. (1) A-skip: high knee, exaggerated skip, 30 yards. (2) B-skip: A-skip plus extend and claw the foot down. (3) Sprint at 70%: 30 yards. (4) Sprint at 90%: 30 yards. (5) All-out sprint: 30 yards. Rest 60 seconds between sprints. Record your time on the final all-out sprint.
cue: Pump your arms. Your legs will follow your arms.
why: Good running form helps on the bases and in the field. Timing your final sprint lets you see progress.
watch: Swinging arms across the body. Arms drive forward and back, not sideways.
harder: Light partner-band resistance for 10-yard starts (older players only).
easier: Just A-skips and then one full-speed sprint.

title: Hip Hinge and Athletic Ready Drill
setup: Stand with feet shoulder-width. No equipment.
how: Stand feet shoulder-width. Push hips backward. NOT bending the knees first. Keep back flat. Hands slide down the thighs. Feel the hamstring stretch. Stand back up by driving hips forward. 15 reps slow. Then: hold the hinge for 3 seconds at the bottom. Then stand in athletic ready position. Same hinge but with knees slightly bent. Hold 10 seconds. 3 times.
cue: Hips back, not knees down. Baseball is played hips back.
why: The hip hinge is the base of the ready position for fielding and hitting. Practicing it on its own makes it easier to find in the game.
watch: Bending the knees first instead of hinging at the hip.
harder: Add a dowel rod along the spine to feel if the back is staying flat.
easier: Stand in front of a wall so the hips push back into it as a reference.

title: Solo Comebacker Drill
setup: Stand 20-25 feet from a wall. Put a tape target on the wall at chest height.
how: Stand 20-25 feet from a wall. Throw a tennis ball at the base of the wall so it comes back fast, like a comebacker. Field it cleanly, set your feet, and make an easy throw to a tape target on the wall. 20 reps. Mix up your throws so rebounds come to your glove side and your throwing side.
cue: Glove up, field it, set your feet, then throw.
why: Balls get hit back at pitchers. This gives solo fielding reps as a pitcher, with no delivery work and very little arm stress.
watch: Turning away from the ball. Rushing the throw before the feet are set.
harder: Move closer for faster rebounds. Use a reaction ball for odd bounces.
easier: Softer throws and stand farther back for slower rebounds.

title: Mound Visualization Routine
setup: Stand on the mound alone, ball in hand. No catcher needed.
how: Stand on the mound alone. 10 dry run-throughs of your routine with no ball. Before each: see the catcher's glove clearly. Picture the pitch hitting that spot. After 10: throw a few real pitches if your pitch count allows, and count them.
cue: See it perfectly. Then throw it.
why: Picturing the target from the spot where you will pitch can help some players feel ready. Imagery has some research support, mostly in older athletes. Keep it short.
watch: Rushing through visualization. Not seeing a specific target. Be precise.
harder: Visualize the most pressured game moment you have faced.
easier: Just 5 visualizations. See the target only.

title: Miss Pattern Chart
gear: Baseball, tape target on wall or net
setup: Mark a 12-inch tape target on a wall or net at strike zone height. Throw from a comfortable distance (30-40 feet).
how: Mark a tape target at strike zone height. Throw 15 pitches at comfortable effort from 30-40 feet. After each: mark left, right, high, low, or on target on a scorecard. After 15: look for a pattern and pick the part of the target to aim at next time. Count these toward your daily pitch total.
cue: Same target, same effort. Just notice where the misses go.
why: Knowing where your misses tend to go makes practice more specific. We track the result, not the delivery. If there is a pattern, a qualified pitching coach can help.
watch: Overthrowing to try to hit the target. Any arm pain: stop.
harder: Smaller target. Chart across several sessions.
easier: Closer (20-25 feet). Bigger target.

title: Between-Play Reset Routine
setup: Build and practice this routine before it's needed in a game.
how: Build this in a quiet moment. Not mid-game. Three steps. Step 1: physical release. One breath, shake out the hands, adjust your hat. Step 2: verbal reset. Say "next play" out loud or in your head. Step 3: refocus cue. Pick one thing to look at that signals you are back (the outfield fence, the mound, the next batter). Practice these three steps 10 times in a row at home before using in a game.
cue: One breath, one word, one look. Then play.
why: Reset routines are a common sport psychology tool. They give a player something simple to do after a mistake instead of stewing. Research support is mostly with older athletes, but it costs nothing to try.
watch: Skipping step 2. The word is the signal that the last play is over.
harder: Use the routine after every out. Not just after errors. Make it automatic.
easier: Just one step: take one slow breath. Add steps after the first feels natural.

title: Self-Talk Reframing Practice
setup: After any bad practice or game, write down the first negative thought you had.
how: After any difficult practice or game: write down the first negative thought. Under it, write the reframe: "[Negative thought] = [What it actually means for next time]." Do this for every negative thought from that session. Not just one. Read the reframes out loud. Put the notebook away.
cue: That happened. What does it mean for next time?
why: Self-talk is one of the better-studied mental skills in sport, mostly with older athletes. Reframing does not deny what happened; it points to what to do next.
watch: Reframes that are just positive spin. Must be actionable.
harder: Reframe in real time during the game. Practice the thought correction as it happens.
easier: Just one thought and one reframe. Start simple.

title: Focus Grid Training
setup: Find or print a 10x10 grid of random numbers 00-99. Set a 1-minute timer.
how: Print a 10x10 grid of random numbers 00-99 or use a focus grid app. Set a 1-minute timer. Find and cross out 00, 01, 02... in sequence as fast as possible. Count how many you find. Record your score. Practice 3 times per week. Track improvement over 3 weeks. Every time your mind wanders: your count drops. This is the immediate feedback.
cue: Stay in the grid. Every time your mind wanders, your count drops.
why: A classic concentration challenge from sport psychology. Evidence that it improves focus in games is weak, so treat it as a fun challenge and a way to practice refocusing.
watch: Jumping to higher numbers. Must go in sequence.
harder: 2-minute sessions. Use a smaller number font.
easier: 30-second sessions. Larger numbers on the grid.

title: Softball Pitcher Target Game
gear: Balls, catcher or net, tape target
setup: Pitcher at the league pitching distance. Catcher or net with a strike zone target.
how: Pitcher calls a spot (in, out, up, down) before each pitch. Catcher holds the glove there. 15 pitches. Hit the spot = 2 points, strike but not the spot = 1 point. Beat your last score. Count every pitch.
cue: Call it, see it, hit it.
why: A target and a score make command practice a game. We keep feedback on the target, not the windmill motion. Leave delivery coaching to a qualified pitching coach.
watch: Throwing harder instead of hitting the spot. Any arm or shoulder pain: stop for the day.
harder: Smaller target zones. A batter stands in (no swing) for realism.
easier: Shorter distance. Bigger target. Two zones only: in and out.

title: High-Zone Target Work
gear: Balls, catcher or net, tape target on net
setup: Tape a target at the top of the strike zone on a net or strike zone board. Pitcher at regulation distance (35-43 feet depending on age).
how: Pitcher aims at the high target only, 15 pitches, using whatever pitch their pitching coach has taught. Mark hits vs. misses. Debrief: where did the misses go? Count every pitch.
cue: Pick the spot and hit it.
why: Hitting the top of the zone on purpose is a useful skill. We keep this about the target; pitch-specific spin and release work belongs with a qualified pitching coach.
watch: Pitches sailing over the target. Trying to throw harder instead of hitting the spot. Any arm pain: stop.
harder: Alternate high and low targets.
easier: 10 pitches at a bigger target.

title: Slap Hitting Footwork
gear: Tee or coach pitch, bases at regulation distance
setup: Left-handed hitter (or a right-handed player learning to slap from the left side) in the batter's box. Tee set up at the front of the zone.
how: Step 1: footwork only. No bat. Crossover step with the back foot, then stride step toward first base. 10 footwork-only reps. Step 2: add the bat, no ball. Swing through the zone with the slap motion. 10 reps. Step 3: add the ball on the tee. Slap 10 balls with full footwork. Time to first base on each rep.
cue: Cross, step, slap. Be running before contact.
why: The slap gets the hitter moving toward first before contact, which puts pressure on the defense. The footwork has to feel natural before contact quality can improve.
watch: Stopping the footwork on contact. Back foot not fully crossing over before the slap.
harder: Live coach pitch. Add a first baseman to create real urgency.
easier: Walk-speed footwork only. Build up to running speed over multiple sessions.

title: Low-Zone Target Work
gear: Balls, catcher or net with low target
setup: Tape a low target at the knees on a net. Pitcher at regulation distance.
how: 15 pitches at the low target only. After each pitch the catcher says "on" or "miss." After 15: where did the misses go? Count every pitch.
cue: Knees. Hit the glove.
why: Low pitches tend to produce ground balls. This keeps the focus on the target; pitch-specific release work belongs with a qualified pitching coach.
watch: Pitches bouncing short. Aiming so hard the pitcher gets tense. Any arm pain: stop.
harder: Alternate low and high targets. A hitter stands in the box (no swing).
easier: Bigger target, shorter distance.

title: Softball Outfield Distances
gear: Balls, gloves, bases or cones marking regulation distances
setup: Fastpitch bases are 60 feet at most youth and high school levels (check your league). Full outfield positions.
how: Coach hits or tosses fly balls and line drives to outfielders. Outfielders throw to the correct base or cutoff. 15 balls total, mixing throws to second and home. Emphasize: plays happen fast on a 60-foot diamond, so get rid of the ball quickly.
cue: Shorter bases, faster plays. Get it in quick.
why: Plays happen fast on a softball diamond. Practicing at real distances helps outfielders learn how quickly they need to get the ball in.
watch: Outfielders holding the ball. High, looping throws that give runners extra time.
harder: Add a live runner. Double cuts for long throws.
easier: Short-distance throws only. Build outward.

title: Pitcher-Catcher Signs Game
setup: Pitcher at the rubber or flat ground. Catcher at league distance.
how: Catcher calls a location with a simple sign before each pitch (inside, outside, up, down). Pitcher reads the sign and pitches to that spot. 15 pitches. A point for each pitch that hits the called location. Count every pitch.
cue: Read the sign, see the glove, hit it.
why: Builds the pitcher-catcher connection and target focus without changing the pitcher's motion. Pitch-specific grips and releases belong with a qualified pitching coach.
watch: Pitcher missing signs. Catcher not holding the target long enough. Any arm pain: stop.
harder: Add a shake-off: pitcher can shake once. Add a batter standing in.
easier: Two locations only. Coach calls the spot out loud instead of a sign.

title: Softball Compressed Diamond Game
gear: Bases at 40-50 ft (youth) or 60 ft (teen), wiffle balls or soft balls
setup: Bases at 40-50 feet for younger players. Coach pitches underhand from 25-30 feet. Three teams.
how: Three-team rotation. Two teams play while one rests. Coach pitches underhand, soft and hittable. One out per batter, 3 outs per inning. Ask "Where's the play?" before each pitch. Rotate every 8 minutes.
cue: See it, then swing hard.
why: Lots of hittable pitches, lots of at-bats, and a small field where kids can make plays. Underhand coach pitch fits the softball game.
watch: Hitters swinging before the ball gets to them. Fielders not setting before the pitch.
harder: Real windmill pitching instead of coach pitch.
easier: Tee hitting only. Just focus on playing the field and running bases.

title: Catcher Blocking Drill
gear: Tennis balls or soft balls, catcher gear, home plate
setup: Catcher in full gear behind home plate. Coach or pitcher throws balls intentionally in the dirt.
how: Coach throws 15 balls. Mix of short hops in front, bounces to the left, and bounces to the right. Catcher drops to both knees on each dirt ball and blocks with the body. Glove fills the five-hole. After blocking: catcher locates the ball and secures it. One point for every ball kept in front of the plate.
cue: Drop and smother. Glove fills the five-hole.
why: Balls in the dirt are common in youth softball. A catcher who keeps them in front stops runners from taking extra bases.
watch: Catcher reaching down instead of dropping to knees. Glove not filling the five-hole (the gap between the legs).
harder: Add a runner at third who tries to score on any ball that gets past.
easier: Tennis balls only. Shorter distance (20 feet).

title: First Base Footwork Drill
setup: First baseman at the bag. Infielder or coach at shortstop position with balls. Runner at home plate.
