how: Infielder throws to first base. Varying location: perfect chest-high, low to the short hop, wide pull to the foul line, high above the bag. First baseman must: find the bag with the foot first, then locate the throw. 15 throws from each infield position. Runner sprints to first on each throw, using the orange safety base if your league has one.
cue: Find the bag with your foot. Then find the ball with your eyes.
why: Finding the bag first, then the ball, keeps first basemen from missing the base. Doing it quickly takes practice.
watch: First baseman leaving the bag too early. Foot position: most coaches teach throwing-side foot on the bag and a stretch toward the throw with the glove-side foot.
harder: Add throws from all four infield positions in a sequence.
easier: No runner. Slow throws only. Walk through the footwork before adding speed.

title: Sacrifice Bunt Execution
setup: Pitcher on mound. Fielders at first and third. Batter in box. Two situations: runner on first, runner on second.
how: Batter squares to bunt as the pitcher begins the delivery, not before. Bat held loosely at the top of the strike zone. Ball must go down: top third of the ball. 10 attempts per batter. Two targets: runner on first, bunt toward the first base line; runner on second, bunt toward the third base line so the third baseman has to field it. Coach calls the target before each pitch.
cue: Top third of the ball. Let it die on the grass.
why: The sacrifice bunt moves runners, and it takes practice to get the ball down in the right spot. A loose grip helps deaden the ball; a stiff grip tends to pop it up.
watch: Squaring before the pitcher commits. Tip to defense. Grip too tight causing pop-ups. Bat below the ball instead of at the top of it.
harder: Live bunt situations with real baserunners and fielders making plays. Squeeze bunt under pressure.
easier: Coach soft-toss at short distance first. Focus on grip and bat angle before adding live pitching.

title: Drag Bunt for a Hit
gear: Balls, pitcher or pitching machine, bases
setup: Pitcher at regulation distance. First base at regulation. Left-handed hitters bunt toward first. Right-handed hitters bunt toward third.
how: Drag bunt timing: wait until the last moment. Bat comes through just as the front foot lands. Do not square. Move the bat to the ball from the regular hitting stance. Ball must pass through the key "dead zone," 15-20 feet up the line, out of reach of both the pitcher and the corner infielder. 10 drag bunts per player. Time to first base.
cue: Late contact. Let it get to you, then bunt.
why: The drag bunt can surprise a defense because the hitter does not square early. A nice tool for fast runners once basic bunting is solid.
watch: Showing the bunt too early. Must look like a swing until the last second. Bunting the ball too hard. Must die in the grass.
harder: Add a fielder who charges hard. Hitter must time the drag to beat the charge.
easier: Tee or slow toss first. Practice the footwork without a ball 10 times.

title: Squeeze Bunt Under Pressure
gear: Full battery, runner on third, fielders
setup: Runner on third. Full battery. Fielders at corners. Coach signals the squeeze before each rep. Safety squeeze (bunt only if it's a strike) vs. suicide squeeze (bunt regardless).
how: Suicide squeeze: runner breaks on the pitch. Batter must bunt anything. Even a ball in the dirt. 8 reps of each type. Debrief after each: did the runner go? Did the batter make contact? If either one fails on a suicide squeeze, the runner is usually out. Treat it like a real game consequence.
cue: Suicide squeeze: bunt the ball or the runner is dead.
why: The squeeze needs the runner and batter to commit together. Practicing it with real stakes builds that trust before game day.
watch: Runner hesitating to break. Batter taking a pitch on a suicide squeeze.
harder: Full live inning with a score. Squeeze is called randomly by coach from the third base box.
easier: Walk-through only: pitcher simulates delivery at half speed. Runner takes two steps. Batter squares and holds the bunt.

title: Bunt Target Drill
gear: Tee or soft toss, cones marking target zones, balls
setup: Mark three cone target zones: Zone 1 (right side, near first base line), Zone 2 (middle, in front of pitcher), Zone 3 (left side, near third base line). Batter works off tee or soft toss.
how: Coach calls the zone before each bunt. Batter squares and directs the bunt to the called zone. 5 bunts per zone, 15 total. Count bunts that land in the target zone. A bunt that goes past the 30-foot cone is too hard. Automatic redo. Compete: can you hit the zone on 10 of 15?
cue: Redirect. Don't push. Angle the bat toward the zone and let the ball come to it.
why: Bunt direction comes from the angle of the bat. Target zones show right away whether the angle was right.
watch: Pushing the bunt. Hands should stay still and ball comes to the bat. Bat face angle inconsistent.
harder: Live pitching with called zones. Add time pressure. Fielder charges from third.
easier: One zone only per session. Mark the bat face angle with tape as a reference.

title: Bunt Defense Rotation
gear: Full infield, pitcher, catcher, balls, runners
setup: Full infield. Runner on first. Coach signals the coverage before each pitch: standard coverage or a first-base crash. Pitcher and corner infielders know their jobs.
how: Standard coverage: 1B charges, 3B charges, pitcher takes everything in the middle, SS covers second, 2B covers first. First-base-only crash: 3B holds near the bag, 1B charges hard, pitcher takes the middle. (The true wheel play has BOTH corners crashing simultaneously. This is a modified, single-corner coverage.) Run 10 bunt situations. Coach hits a bunt after signaling coverage. Fielders execute. Debrief: who had the ball? Was the throw to the right base?
cue: Pitcher: call the play. Corner fielders: charge on the pitch, not after.
why: Bunt defense breaks down when nobody knows their job. Calling the coverage before the pitch gives everyone an assignment.
watch: Corner infielders not charging until after the bunt. Must charge on the pitch. Pitcher not making the verbal call.
harder: Add runners on first and second. Add a runner on third for squeeze defense.
easier: Walk through each coverage type without a bunt first. Walk, don't run, the first 5 reps.

title: First and Third Defense Calls
gear: Full infield, runners at first and third
setup: Runners at first and third. Full infield. Defense must make a pre-pitch call: which play they are running if the runner steals.
how: Four defensive options, called before every pitch: (1) Catcher throws through to second. (2) Catcher throws to a middle infielder cutting in front of second, who can cut it and throw home if the runner at third breaks. (3) Catcher fakes to second and looks or throws to third. (4) Catcher holds the ball and concedes second base. Run 10 live situations. Runners decide randomly whether to steal. Defense executes the called play.
cue: Make the call before the pitch. Commit to it.
why: First and third gets chaotic when nobody has an assignment. One pre-pitch call gives everyone a job.
watch: Defense changing the call mid-pitch. Shortstop not setting up in the cut position.
harder: Offense can call their own plays. Creates genuine game-speed decision-making.
easier: Walk through each play type without live runners first. Two options only before adding all four.

title: Structured Batting Practice Rotation
gear: Full field, pitcher or pitching machine, L-screen, balls
setup: Standard BP rotation: hitter in the box, on-deck circle, shagger in left field, shagger in right field, shagger in center, pitcher, catcher. Everyone rotates after each hitter's turn.
how: Each hitter gets one round of 10 pitches. Round structure: 2 bunts, 2 hit-and-run (swing at anything), 2 opposite field, 4 free swings. Coach announces each segment before the pitch. Hitter focuses on the assigned task. Not just putting the ball in play. After 10 pitches: rotate immediately. Total time: 25 minutes for a full team.
cue: Every pitch has a job. Know your job before it leaves the pitcher's hand.
why: Giving each pitch a job makes batting practice more purposeful than just swinging. Hitters get in the habit of knowing their task before the pitch.
watch: Hitters treating all 10 pitches the same. No adjustment on opposite-field pitches.
harder: Add a competitive element: points for executing the assigned task. Pitcher changes location without warning.
easier: Three categories only: bunt, away pitch, free swing. Build from there.

title: Cage Situational Hitting
gear: Pitching machine or partner, batting cage or net, balls
setup: Hitter in cage or net setup. Coach or partner feeds pitches. Before each round: coach announces a game situation.
how: Situation 1: "Runner on third, one out, you need a fly ball." Hitter works on driving the ball deep. Situation 2: "Runner on second, nobody out, move the runner." Hitter works on right-side ground balls. Situation 3: "0-2 count. Protect the plate." Hitter works on two-strike approach: hands inside, contact deep in the zone. 5 pitches per situation, 3 situations per round.
cue: What does this at-bat need. Not what do you want to do.
why: Different situations call for different swings. Practicing them in the cage gives hitters a plan they can use in games.
watch: Hitter ignoring the situation and just swinging the same way.
harder: Add score and inning context: "Down two, seventh inning, runner on second." Changes urgency entirely.
easier: One situation type per full session. Master it before rotating.

title: Pickoff Move to First
gear: Ball, first baseman, runner at first
setup: Pitcher at the rubber. First baseman at the bag. Runner taking a lead at first. Use only where leads and pickoffs are allowed (not Little League 12U and younger).
how: Pitcher works from the stretch. Mix in pickoff attempts. Right-hander has two legal options: (1) step off the rubber with the pivot foot first, then throw; or (2) spin move: step toward first base with the free foot and spin to throw. Both are legal. Left-hander can make a legal pickoff move directly from the set position. Run 10 total: 6 pitches to the plate, 4 pickoff attempts (randomized so the runner can't predict). After each pickoff: debrief the runner. "Did you get back? What did you see?"
cue: Righties: step off the rubber first, or step directly toward first. Learn the step-off first.
why: A legal, consistent pickoff move keeps runners honest and helps pitchers avoid balks. Learning the legal footwork is the main goal.
watch: Right-handed pitcher throwing to first without a legal step toward the base or stepping off first. Balk. Remind: must either step off the rubber first, or execute a legal spin step toward the base. Not varying timing between pitches and pickoffs.
harder: Runner attempts to steal. Pitcher must decide pitch or pickoff in real time.
easier: Walk through the step-off footwork 20 times without a throw. Ingrain the footwork before adding the throw.

title: Pickoff Play to Second
gear: Full battery, shortstop and second baseman, runner at second
setup: Runner at second. Pitcher at the rubber. Shortstop and second baseman at their positions. Pre-game signal established: who is covering on the daylight play.
how: Run the daylight play: shortstop breaks toward second, pitcher turns and throws when they see daylight between the runner and shortstop. Alternate with 2B covering. 8 reps. Mix in real pitches to home. Runner reads pitch vs. pickoff. Establish the look-off: pitcher looks toward second, SS fakes, runner leans. Then throw.
cue: See the daylight. Then throw. Don't throw on the SS break.
why: The daylight play can catch a relaxed runner at second. It needs timing between pitcher and shortstop, so it takes practice.
watch: Throwing on the shortstop's break before daylight exists. No look-off to sell the play.
harder: Live stolen base attempt. Pitcher must recognize and either pitch or pick.
easier: Walk through the timing in slow motion. Pitcher and shortstop count together: "1, break, daylight, throw."

title: Baserunning Sprint Circuit
setup: Full base set at regulation distances. Players in batting stance at home plate. Two groups race.
how: Rep 1: Sprint home to first. Timed. Rep 2: Sprint home to second. Round first correctly. Rep 3: Sprint home to third. Round both bases correctly. Rep 4: Inside-the-park home run. All four bases, correct arc on every bag. Rest 90 seconds between each rep. Track times. Post them. Compete to beat your personal best each week.
cue: Attack every base. Never glide.
why: Timed runs give players a number to beat and a reason to round bases correctly. Tracking personal bests keeps it about their own progress.
watch: Sloppy rounding on the second and third rep. Players jogging back after each rep. Walk back to stay ready.
harder: Compare times running a straight line vs. a good arc.
easier: One base only. Walk the correct arc path before sprinting.

title: Down and Back Baserunning
gear: Bases or cones at regulation distance
setup: Bases at regulation distance. Players at home. Two lines run simultaneously.
how: On "go": sprint to first and back (touching the bag each time). Then sprint to second and back. Then to third and back. Then full circuit. Home to first to second to third to home. No resting between distances. Straight through. First player to complete all four distances wins. Run 3 full competitions.
cue: Touch the bag every time. A missed bag is a missed out.
why: A classic start-and-stop running game. Short sprints with changes of direction look a lot like how baseball players actually run.
watch: Missing bases during competition. Players half-sprinting. Enforce full effort.
harder: Winner picks the next warm-up game.
easier: One distance only: home to first and back. Build from there.

title: Full Pregame Routine
gear: Full infield and outfield, fungo, balls
setup: Full field. Two fungos. One for infield, one for outfield. Coach hits. Standard pre-game sequence.
how: One standard sequence (about 12 minutes; adapt to your league's available time): (1) Outfield fly balls and throws to third. 2 minutes. (2) Outfield throws to second. 1 minute. (3) Outfield throws to cutoff home. 1 minute. (4) Infield grounders to each position, throw to first. 2 minutes. (5) Around the horn. 1 minute each direction. (6) Infield double play feeds. 2 minutes. (7) Final around the horn, catcher returns to pitcher. 1 minute. Run this until the team can complete it under 12 minutes without errors.
cue: Pre-game is not warm-up. It's a statement. Own it.
why: A clean pregame routine gets everyone moving and focused before the first pitch. When kids know it well, it runs itself.
watch: Slow transitions between segments. Enforce urgency. Cutoff man not setting up correctly.
harder: Time the full routine and challenge the team to complete it faster without errors.
easier: Run one segment at a time until each is clean before combining into the full sequence.

title: Sign Reading and Execution
setup: Coach at third base. Two players: one batter, one runner on first. Establish a simple sign sequence before starting.
how: Coach flashes a full sign sequence (indicator, sign, wipe-off). Batter must decode the sign and repeat it back verbally before the pitch. Start with a two-touch indicator sequence. Progress to a three-touch sequence. Run 20 sign reads. Mix of real signs (steal, hit and run, bunt, take) and decoys. Batter and runner must both execute the same sign independently.
cue: Find the indicator first. Everything before it is noise.
why: Reading signs is a skill that needs practice. Players who have never practiced signs under a little pressure are more likely to miss them in games.
watch: Batter reading only the indicator and missing the actual sign. Runner and batter executing different signs.
harder: Increase sequence length to four touches. Add a hot sign (automatic steal regardless of the sequence).
easier: One sign only (steal) with a one-touch indicator. Walk through 10 times before adding complexity.

title: Catch Play Scoring Game
setup: Partners start 30 feet apart. This is catch with a scoring game, not a throwing program.
how: Partners play catch at comfortable distances. Score each throw: chest = 2 points, catchable without moving the feet = 1. First pair to 21 wins. Comfortable effort only. Follow your league and Pitch Smart guidance on total throwing and rest.
cue: Hit the chest. Every throw has a target.
why: Turns warm-up catch into a game with a target on every throw. Kids pay more attention when throws are scored. Keep effort comfortable and stop for any arm pain.
watch: Throwing max effort for distance. Anyone rubbing an arm or saying it hurts: stop and tell a parent.
harder: Quick-release round: points only if the throw leaves within 2 seconds of the catch. Pairs may move back 15 feet after each game if both are comfortable.
easier: Stay at 30-45 feet. Tennis balls for younger players.

title: Shortstop and Third Base Range Drill
setup: Shortstop and third baseman at their positions. Coach with fungo at home. First baseman at the bag.
how: 10 balls to each player, mixed: (1) Hard shot directly at the player. (2) Slow roller in the hole. (3) Hard shot up the middle. SS only. (4) Bunt or slow roller down the third base line. 3B only. (5) Pop-up in the short outfield. Communication required. After each fielded ball: throw to first, time the play. Debrief after each group of 5 balls: "What read did you make before the ball was hit?"
cue: Set your feet before the pitch. Not during the play.
why: Range on the left side of the infield comes from positioning before the pitch, a good first step, and a good route. Asking about the read before the ball is hit trains the first part.
watch: Players flat-footed at pitch. Must be on balls of feet in ready position.
harder: Add a runner. Fielder must beat the runner. Add decision: SS must decide between throwing to second vs. first.
easier: Coach rolls grounders slowly first. Drop step and route only. No throw.

title: Catcher Framing and Receiving
gear: Full catcher gear, balls, pitcher or pitching machine
setup: Catcher in full gear behind home plate. Pitcher at regulation distance or pitching machine set to consistent location.
how: Three receiving focuses. 5 pitches each: (1) Framing the edge pitch. Glove moves to present the pitch: inward for outside-corner pitches, upward for low pitches, hold steady for pitches in the heart. The direction is location-specific, not one universal movement. (2) Blocking. Glove fills the five-hole, body drops on dirt balls. (3) Pop time. Receive, transfer, throw to second. Time the pop time and try to beat your own best. Total: 15 pitches. Catcher calls each pitch a ball or strike as they receive it.
cue: Receive first. Frame second. The catch earns the call.
why: Clean receiving helps the umpire see the pitch and cuts down on passed balls. Stabbing at the ball makes close pitches harder to call.
watch: Glove moving before the catch. Must receive then frame. Pop-time footwork: feet must drive toward second on the throw.
harder: Mix pitch locations randomly. Catcher must adjust receive and frame for every zone.
easier: Soft toss at 20 feet. One focus only: catching location before adding framing.

title: Slump Protocol
gear: Notebook or phone, video of own previous at-bats
setup: Player in a quiet space, ideally with a coach. No field needed. Used when a player is in an 0-for-10 or longer hitting drought.
how: Step 1: Review. Watch 5 at-bats from before the slump and 5 during. Identify one mechanical difference without judgment. Step 2: Reset. Identify one process goal for the next 3 at-bats only (not the whole season). Step 3: Return. Take 20 tee swings at the corrected position at 70% effort before the next game. Step 4: Compress the zone mentally. Expect to hit the ball somewhere on the field, not everywhere. One simple approach: sit fastball, react to off-speed.
cue: One swing. Next pitch.
why: Slumps are partly mental. Players tend to overthink and tighten up. This shrinks the goal to the next few at-bats and one process focus.
watch: Player setting a goal for too long a time frame. Must be "next 3 at-bats," not "this week."
harder: After successful at-bats using the protocol: debrief what worked. Build the personal slump-breaker into the pre-game routine.
easier: Just one step: set one process goal for the next at-bat only. Nothing else.

title: Pre-Game Mental Preparation
setup: 15-20 minutes before the game. Player alone or with team in a quiet environment. Not during warm-up. Before it.
how: Three-step sequence: (1) Activation. 2 minutes. Set one process goal for today's game: one behavior, not one outcome. Write it on your wrist tape. (2) Visualization. 3 minutes. Eyes closed. Two at-bats, two defensive plays. See them succeed. Feel the contact. Hear the sound. (3) Anchor. 1 minute. Recall your best performance memory. Hold it for 60 seconds. Walk to warm-up from that mental state.
cue: Process goal on the wrist. Best memory in the head. Go play.
why: Routines, imagery, and process goals are common sport psychology tools with research support, mostly in older athletes. A simple pregame plan gives teens something steady to lean on.
watch: Players rushing through. 6 minutes minimum. Outcome goals instead of process goals.
harder: Build a full written pre-game routine card the player carries in their bag.
easier: Just the process goal step. One sentence on the wrist. Build from there.
